Course Information

Course overview

Course overview

This course has been structured for online and blended learning. Synchronous and asynchronous work has been developed, including discussions, activities and reflections. In person sessions will also be organised throughout the year to compliment the online course.

The Canvas course will also incorporate other interactive features such as quizzes, multimedia and recordings from a range of staff and experts in the relevant fields. 

Formative feedback will be embedded throughout the course to accompany the mandated summative assessment tasks that students will complete.

Please post and reply to the questions of others throughout the year. 

Expectations

The Year 12 course requires 120 indicative hours including both synchronous and asynchronous learning and working towards the completion of each assessment task.

The course modules have been 'chunked' into 2 week cycles. A cycle represents a typical school fortnight of 8 hours of class time for a subject. Each cycle therefore represents the amount of work you would be expected to complete during the 8 hours of class you would have sat face to face.

Year 12 Indicative Hours
Secure Software Architecture 30
Programming for the Web 30
Software Automation 30
Software Engineering Project     30

You are expected to behave respectfully while online and face to face. You can email the course coordinator, mienna@kings.edu.au if you have any concerns throughout the year.

Learning Outcomes

  • SE-12-01 justifies methods used to plan, develop and engineer software solutions
  • SE-12-02 applies structural elements to develop programming code
  • SE-12-03 analyses how current hardware, software and emerging technologies influence the development of software engineering solutions
  • SE-12-04 evaluates practices to safely and securely collect, use and store data
  • SE-12-05 explains the social, ethical and legal implications of software engineering on the individual, society and the environment
  • SE-12-06 justifies the selection and use of tools and resources to design, develop, manage and evaluate software
  • SE-12-07 designs, develops and implements safe and secure programming solutions
  • SE-12-08 tests and evaluates language structures to refine code
  • SE-12-09 applies methods to manage and document the development of a software project

NESA

Components and weightings for Year 12:

Performance band descriptors for Software Engineering

HSC performance band descriptions summarise the knowledge, understanding and skills typically demonstrated by students at each band level in a particular course. NESA uses these holistic descriptions to report a student's overall level of achievement in an HSC course.

Band 6

A student who typically performs at this level:

  • demonstrates comprehensive understanding of the influence of technologies on the development of software engineering solutions

  • demonstrates extensive knowledge and understanding of the social, ethical and legal implications of the application of software engineering solutions on the individual, society and the environment

  • applies sophisticated technical skills in the design and implementation of programming solutions

  • collects, uses, manages and stores complex data effectively, safely and securely

  • applies comprehensive skills in developing, managing and documenting software engineering projects

  • communicates logically and effectively using a range of terms, conventions and methods

Band 5

A student who typically performs at this level:

  • demonstrates broad understanding of the influence of technologies on the development of software engineering solutions

  • demonstrates thorough knowledge and understanding of the social, ethical and legal implications of the application of software engineering solutions on the individual, society and the environment

  • applies high-level technical skills in the design and implementation of programming solutions

  • collects, uses, manages and stores data effectively, safely and securely

  • demonstrates high-level skills in developing, managing and documenting software engineering projects

  • communicates logically, using appropriate terms, conventions and methods

Band 4

A student who typically performs at this level:

  • demonstrates sound understanding of the influence of technologies on the development of software engineering solutions

  • demonstrates sound knowledge and understanding of the social, ethical and legal implications of the application of software engineering solutions

  • applies sound technical skills in the design and implementation of programming solutions

  • collects, uses, manages and stores data safely and securely

  • demonstrates sound skills in developing, managing and documenting software engineering projects

  • communicates using relevant terms, conventions and methods

Band 3

A student who typically performs at this level:

  • demonstrates basic understanding of the influence of technologies on the development of software engineering solutions

  • demonstrates basic knowledge and understanding of the social and/or ethical and/or legal implications of the application of software engineering solutions

  • displays basic skills in programming

  • uses data safely and securely

  • displays basic skills in developing software engineering projects

  • communicates using basic terms and conventions and/or methods

Band 2

A student who typically performs at this level:

  • demonstrates limited understanding of the use of technologies

  • displays limited skills in programming

  • displays limited skills in developing software engineering projects

  • communicates with limited use of terms

Band 1

Performance at a lower level than Band 2 is reported as Band 1.

Cycle 1 (Term 4: Weeks 1-2) Secure Software Architecture

Introduction to Cycle 1

  Introduction

This module will focus on the importance of developing secure software, and how following structured software development steps can ensure the security, reliability, and performance of your programs. In addition to learning about secure development practices, you’ll explore how software design concepts such as confidentiality, integrity, and availability play a crucial role in creating secure systems. The topics in this module will guide you through the software development process, from initial requirements to deployment and maintenance, with a strong emphasis on security. By the end, you’ll also understand how the end user’s capabilities influence secure design features.

  Syllabus

Designing Software

  • Describe the benefits of developing secure software

    Including:
    • data protection
    • minimising cyber attacks and vulnerabilities

  • Interpret and apply fundamental software development steps to develop secure code

    Including:
    • requirements definition
    • determining specifications
    • design
    • development
    • integration
    • testing and debugging
    • installation
    • maintenance

  • Describe how the capabilities and experience of end users influence the secure design features of software

Developing secure code

  • Explore fundamental software design security concepts when developing programming code

    Including:
    • confidentiality
    • integrity
    • availability
    • authentication
    • authorisation
    • accountability

  • Apply security features incorporated into software including data protection, security, privacy and regulatory compliance

 

  Discussion

Before diving into this module, reflect on your understanding of secure software development. Share in the comment box below any experience you have with developing secure code or your thoughts on the importance of security in software development. How do you think secure practices affect the overall software development process?

1.1 Secure Code Benefits

Syllabus
Describe the benefits of developing secure software, including:
- data protection
- minimising cyber attacks and vulnerabilities

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the importance of developing secure software.
  • Identify the key benefits of secure software development, including data protection and minimising cyber attacks and vulnerabilities.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to describe the key benefits of secure software development.
  • Students will be able to explain how secure software protects data and reduces the risk of cyber-attacks and vulnerabilities.

Content

Benefits of Developing Secure Software

Developing secure software is crucial in today's digital landscape, where threats to data and systems are constantly evolving. Secure software development focuses on building applications that protect sensitive information and are resilient against malicious activities. This approach safeguards users and organisations and enhances the overall trustworthiness and reliability of software products.

 

Data Protection

Data protection is one of the most significant benefits of secure software development. In an era where data breaches are increasingly common, protecting sensitive information has become paramount. Secure software ensures that data is handled and stored to prevent unauthorised access, manipulation, or loss. Key aspects of data protection in secure software include:

Encryption

   Definition

Encryption is the process of converting data into a code to prevent unauthorised access. It ensures that information is only accessible to those with the correct decryption key and unreadable to anyone without that key.

 

Example:
A financial application encrypts user data, such as credit card numbers and bank account details, using AES-256 encryption. This ensures that the encrypted data remains unreadable and secure even if the data is intercepted during transmission or if someone gains unauthorised access to the storage systems.

Access Controls

   Definition

Access controls are security measures that regulate who can view or modify data within a system. These controls enforce rules based on user roles or permissions, ensuring that sensitive information is only accessible to authorised individuals.

 

Example:
A healthcare system uses role-based access control (RBAC) to restrict access to patient records. Only authorised personnel, such as doctors and nurses, can view or update a patient's medical information. Administrative staff may have limited access to certain data, such as billing information, without being able to see sensitive medical details.

Data Integrity

    Definition

Data integrity refers to the accuracy and consistency of data over its lifecycle. It involves protecting data from being altered or corrupted and ensuring that it remains reliable and trustworthy from its creation to its final use.

 

Example:
An e-commerce platform uses hash functions, such as SHA-256, to verify the integrity of transactions. Each transaction is hashed, and the resulting hash is compared before and after the data is transmitted. If the hashes match, it confirms that the transaction data has not been altered during transmission. If they don't match, it indicates potential tampering, and the transaction can be flagged for further investigation.

 

 

Minimising Cyber Attacks and Vulnerabilities 

Minimising cyber attacks and vulnerabilities is a critical aspect of secure software development. Cyber attacks can devastate individuals and organisations, leading to data breaches, financial loss, and damage to reputation. Developers can create more secure and resilient applications by proactively addressing vulnerabilities during software development. Some ways in which developers/companies can minimise cyber attacks and vulnerabilities are:

Regular Security Audits

   Definition

Security audits involve a comprehensive review of the software's code, architecture, and processes to identify potential security weaknesses. Regular audits help ensure that vulnerabilities are detected and addressed before being exploited.

 

Example:
A large e-commerce company conducts quarterly security audits of its platform. During these audits, security experts review the codebase for potential vulnerabilities, such as outdated libraries or improper user input handling. These audits have helped the company identify and fix several security issues before attackers could exploit them.

Secure Coding Practices

   Definition

Secure coding practices are a set of guidelines and techniques developers follow to write code resistant to common vulnerabilities. These practices are designed to prevent issues like SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and buffer overflows.

 

Example:
A web application development team follows secure coding practices by validating all user inputs before processing them. For instance, they use prepared statements for database queries to prevent SQL injection attacks. This practice ensures that malicious inputs cannot be used to manipulate the database.

Patch Management

   Definition

Patch management is the process of regularly updating software to fix known vulnerabilities. It involves applying patches provided by software vendors to address security flaws that attackers could exploit.

 

Example:
An organisation uses an automated patch management system to keep all its software current. When a new security patch is released, the system automatically applies the patch to all relevant systems. This approach helps the organisation minimise the risk of cyber attacks that exploit known vulnerabilities.

1.2 Software Development Steps

Syllabus
Interpret and apply fundamental software development steps to develop secure code: 
- requirements definition
- determining specifications 
- design
- development
- integration
- testing and debugging
- installation
- maintenance 

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the fundamental steps of software development necessary for creating secure code.
  • Apply these steps in alignment with the NSW Year 12 Software Engineering syllabus to ensure secure software development.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to describe each step in the software development lifecycle (SDLC) and its associated documentation.
  • Students will be able to explain how each step contributes to developing secure code.
  • Students will be able to apply these steps in practical scenarios, ensuring software security and compliance with the syllabus.

  Content

Developing secure software occurs in each major step of the software development life cycle, preventing vulnerabilities from being introduced. By addressing security during planning, design, development, testing, and maintenance, developers can create robust, resilient software that protects against threats and maintains user trust.

Requirements Definition

Definition:
The definition of requirements involves gathering and documenting the software's functional and non-functional requirements, with a strong focus on security needs.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Client Scenario:
    Understanding the client's needs and expectations regarding security features. This involves meeting with the client to discuss their requirements and the potential security threats relevant to their specific context.

  • Environment Specifications:
    Defining the operational environment, including hardware, software, and network considerations, to ensure security compatibility. This step involves assessing the current environment to identify any security gaps that must be addressed.

  • List of Objectives:
    Creating a comprehensive list of security objectives that the software must achieve. This includes setting specific, measurable goals such as data encryption, access controls, and compliance with regulatory standards.

Determining Specifications

Definition:
Determining specifications involves creating a detailed description of the software's functionality and technical requirements, focusing on how it will meet the defined security needs.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Technical Requirements:
    Defining specific technical details, such as encryption standards, authentication methods, and data handling protocols. These requirements form the technical backbone of the software, ensuring that security measures are robust and effective.

  • Performance Criteria:
    Establishing security-related performance benchmarks, such as response times for security features and the capacity to handle security events, ensures that the software performs efficiently while maintaining a high level of security.

  • Compliance Standards:
    Identifying and incorporating relevant security compliance standards that the software must adhere to. This involves ensuring the software meets industry-specific regulations and standards, such as GDPR or PCI DSS.

  • IPO Model:
    Defining the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model clearly articulates how data inputs will be processed and what secure outputs will be generated. This model helps understand how data flows through the system and where security controls need to be applied.

  • Gantt Charts:
    Developing a Gantt chart to plan and schedule the various tasks involved in developing secure code. The Gantt chart provides a visual timeline of the project, helping to ensure that each task is completed on time and security milestones are met.

Design

Definition:
The design phase involves creating a blueprint for the software, including architecture, data flow, and user interfaces, while embedding security principles.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • System Architecture:
    Designing a secure architecture that incorporates layers of security, such as firewalls, encryption, and secure access points. This step ensures that the software's overall structure is designed to protect against potential security threats.

  • Modelling Tools:

    • Structure Chart:
      Used to represent the hierarchy and relationships between modules in the software, ensuring that secure data flow and control mechanisms are clearly defined.

    • Class Diagram:
      Represents the system's classes, attributes, methods, and relationships, with attention to secure data handling and encapsulation of sensitive information.

    • Data Flow Diagram (DFD):
      Maps out how data moves through the system, identifying where data must be protected during transmission and processing.

    • User Interface Design:
      Ensuring the user interface supports secure interactions, including secure login processes and protection against unauthorised access.

    • Storyboards:
      Creating visual storyboards to represent how users interact with the software, focusing on secure navigation and user experience. Storyboards help design intuitive, secure interfaces by visualising user flows.

    • Data Dictionaries:
      Developing a data dictionary to document all the data elements used in the software, including their definitions, formats, and relationships. The data dictionary ensures that data is consistently and securely handled throughout the system.

    • Pseudocode:
      Writing pseudocode to outline the logic and flow of the program in a human-readable format. Pseudocode helps ensure that security measures, such as input validation and error handling, are planned and implemented correctly.

  • Logbooks:
    Maintaining a logbook to document decisions, design changes, and security considerations throughout the design phase. The logbook records the design process, helping to track security-related decisions and ensuring that all security aspects are thoroughly documented.

Development

Definition:
The development phase is where the software is coded, with an emphasis on secure coding practices to prevent vulnerabilities.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Secure Coding Standards:
    Implementing coding practices that protect against vulnerabilities such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and buffer overflows. This ensures that the code is inherently secure and resistant to attacks.

  • Version Control:
    Using version control systems to track changes and ensure that secure coding practices are consistently applied. Version control allows developers to manage code changes effectively, ensuring that security is maintained throughout development.

  • Code Review:
    Conducting peer reviews of code to identify and address potential security issues before they are integrated into the main codebase. Code reviews help catch security flaws early, reducing the risk of vulnerabilities in the final product.

Integration

Definition:
Integration involves combining individual components into a fully functioning system and ensuring that security controls work across the system.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Component Compatibility:
    Ensuring that all components interact securely and that security measures are effective across the entire system. This step verifies that security features are not compromised when components are combined.

  • Integration Testing:
    Performing tests to verify that security features function correctly when different components are combined. Integration testing ensures that the system is secure and that no vulnerabilities are introduced during integration.

  • Security Verification:
    Conducting a final check to ensure that all integrated components meet the security objectives defined in the requirements stage. This verification step confirms the software is secure before moving on to the next phase.

Testing and Debugging

Definition:
Testing and debugging involve identifying and resolving issues, focusing on uncovering security vulnerabilities.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Security Testing:
    Implementing various testing methods to identify and exploit potential vulnerabilities, including:

    • Static Application Security Testing (SAST):
      SAST analyses the source code for security vulnerabilities without executing the code. It helps identify coding errors that could lead to security flaws.

    • Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST):
      Testing the running application for security vulnerabilities in a live environment. DAST helps detect vulnerabilities that are not visible in the source code alone.

    • Vulnerability Scanning:
      Scanning the application and environment for known vulnerabilities. This step identifies potential weaknesses that attackers could exploit.

    • Penetration Testing:
      Simulating attacks to discover potential vulnerabilities in the system. Penetration testing helps assess the system's ability to withstand real-world attack scenarios.

    • Regression Testing:
      Ensuring that new updates or changes have not introduced new vulnerabilities. Regression testing verifies that the software remains secure after modifications.

    • User Acceptance Testing (UAT):
      Verifying that the software meets security requirements and is ready for deployment. UAT ensures that the final product is secure and functional according to user expectations.

  • Debugging:
    Address any identified security issues and ensure that all vulnerabilities are resolved before deployment. Debugging is essential for fixing security flaws that could compromise the system.

  • Final Security Assessment:
    Conduct a comprehensive review to confirm the software is secure and ready for release. This assessment provides the final check before the software is deployed to production.

Installation

Definition:
The installation phase involves deploying the software in a production environment, ensuring it is securely configured.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Secure Configuration:
    Applying secure settings during installation, such as setting strong passwords, disabling unnecessary services, and configuring firewalls. Secure configuration helps prevent unauthorised access and ensures the system is protected from the start.

  • Deployment Procedures:
    Follow best practices for secure deployment, including ensuring that all data is encrypted during the installation process. Proper deployment procedures help maintain the software's integrity and confidentiality.

  • Post-Installation Testing:
    Tests will be performed after installation to verify that the software is functioning securely in its new environment. This step ensures that the system remains secure after deployment and that no new vulnerabilities have been introduced.

Maintenance

Definition:
Maintenance involves ongoing updates and software monitoring to address new security threats.

Relevant Steps in This Stage:

  • Security Patching:
    Apply updates and patches regularly to fix any newly discovered vulnerabilities. Security patching is critical for keeping the software protected against emerging threats.

  • Monitoring:
    Continuously monitoring the software for security breaches or unusual activity. Monitoring helps detect potential security incidents early, allowing for a quick response.

  • Incident Response:
    Having a plan to respond to security incidents promptly minimises the impact of any breaches. An effective incident response plan ensures that security incidents are managed efficiently and the system can recover quickly.

1.3 End Users

Syllabus
Describe how the capabilities and experience of end users influence the secure design features of software.

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand how the capabilities and experience of end users influence the design of secure software.
  • Identify key considerations in designing secure and user-friendly software for different end users.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to describe how end users' abilities and experience levels impact the security features integrated into software design.
  • Students will be able to explain the balance between usability and security in software design.

  Content

How End Users Influence Secure Design Features of Software

The design of secure software is significantly influenced by the capabilities and experience of its end users. Developers must consider how users interact with the software and ensure that security features are appropriately tailored to suit their needs and abilities. Understanding the user base is crucial to creating software that is both secure and accessible.

User Capabilities

Definition:
User capabilities refer to the technical skills and knowledge that end users possess. These capabilities vary widely, from novice users with minimal technical experience to expert users with advanced knowledge.

Impact on Secure Design Features:

  • Simplified Security Controls:
    Security features must be straightforward to use for users with limited technical skills. This might involve automating complex security tasks, providing clear instructions, and designing intuitive interfaces.

  • Guided Processes:
    Software should guide users through security-related processes, such as setting up two-factor authentication or managing permissions, to ensure they do not inadvertently compromise security.

  • Role-Based Access:
    Implementing role-based access controls can help tailor security features to the user's level of expertise, granting more power to experienced users while limiting potential risks for less experienced users.

User Experience Levels

Definition:
User experience levels refer to users' familiarity and comfort with similar software or security practices. Users with varying experience levels may require different approaches to secure design.

Impact on Secure Design Features:

  • Customisable Security Settings:
    Users may prefer customisable security settings to tailor the software to their specific needs, such as adjusting privacy settings or selecting encryption methods.

  • Default Security Settings:
    For less experienced users, it is essential to provide secure default settings that protect the user without requiring extensive configuration. These settings should be robust enough to prevent common security issues while remaining easy to use.

  • Training and Support:
    Providing training materials and support options helps users of all experience levels understand and utilise the software's security features. This might include tutorials, help guides, or customer support services.

Usability vs. Security

Definition:
Balancing usability with security is a key challenge in software design. While security is paramount, the software must also be usable by its intended audience.

Impact on Secure Design Features:

  • Minimising User Friction:
    Security Minimising Should be integrated to minimise disruption to the user experience. This includes streamlining authentication processes, reducing the steps required to access secure areas, and ensuring that security does not hinder productivity.

  • Transparency of Security Features:
    Users should be aware of the security features, but these features should not be overly intrusive. Providing straightforward but non-intrusive notifications about security events or updates helps keep users informed without overwhelming them.

  • Adaptive Security:
    Adaptive security measures can be adjusted based on user behaviour and risk levels. For example, the software might prompt additional verification if unusual activity is detected, balancing ease of use with heightened security when necessary.

  • Students will be able to implement these concepts in a Python (Flask) web application.

  Content

Several fundamental concepts are crucial in secure software design for ensuring that applications are safe, reliable, and resilient against threats. Below, we explore these concepts and demonstrate how to implement them in a Flask web application.

 

Confidentiality

Definition:
Confidentiality ensures that sensitive information is accessible only to those authorised to view it. In web applications, this often involves encrypting data and securing communications.

Explanation:
This example demonstrates ensuring confidentiality by encrypting data before storing or transmitting it. Flask handles the request and the cryptography library is used to encrypt and decrypt data.

Below is an example of an API request to encrypt and decrypt data. 

$ python3 encryption_test.py
Original Data: Ianni's extremely safe password
Encrypted Data: gAAAAABnFxc7HahGOnsH1tHh2_Od2Gxql2M3kf9v2hGv19PiJ4yLC8ROcdy2jIzT1QY1lWHiaMgwOOUKE899WmGskPiG6LlVKrxUpnbIiynAI5nAqsE281c=

Decrypting your encrypted data is: Ianni's extremely safe password

Integrity

Definition:
Integrity ensures that data is accurate and has not been tampered with. Flask applications can be implemented using hashing algorithms to verify data integrity.

Explanation:
This example ensures data integrity by hashing data and verifying that the hash matches the original data. If the data is altered, the hash will not match, indicating a potential breach of integrity.

This example code sends a string to the /hash API endpoint, which generates a SHA-256 hash of the data. Then, it sends the original string and the hash (generated from the original string) to the /verify endpoint to check if the hash matches, confirming whether the data is intact or altered.

$ python3 integrity_test.py
Original Data: Ianni's extremely safe password
Hashed Data: 025a003603dd8d67442725058507fa5b859ec7d1d911fcfac291c2988fb71a59
Verification Result: Data is intact

Availability

Definition:
Availability ensures that systems and data are accessible to authorised users when needed. Flask can address this by implementing rate limiting to prevent denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

Explanation:
Rate limiting in this Flask application helps ensure availability by restricting the number of requests a user can make, protecting the application from being overwhelmed by excessive traffic.

The @app.errorhandler(429) decorator defines a custom error handler in Flask that specifies how to handle requests that trigger a 429 'Too Many Requests' error. 

The code below makes 11 attempts to access the /resource route. The first 10 requests succeed, but the 11th fails because the API call limit is set to 10 per minute.

$ python3 availability_test.py
Request 1: Resource accessed successfully
Request 2: Resource accessed successfully
Request 3: Resource accessed successfully
Request 4: Resource accessed successfully
Request 5: Resource accessed successfully
Request 6: Resource accessed successfully
Request 7: Resource accessed successfully
Request 8: Resource accessed successfully
Request 9: Resource accessed successfully
Request 10: Resource accessed successfully
Request 11: Failed with status code 429 - Too many requests. Please wait and try again later.

Authentication

Definition:
Authentication is the process of verifying a user's identity. Flask can implement this using a simple username and password system.

Explanation:
This example demonstrates user authentication using hashed passwords. The user's password is hashed for storage, and the login process checks the entered password against the stored hash.

The code below sends a login for a valid user (inside the user dictionary) as defined in authentication.py. The login API will authenticate the user if the password entered matches the one stored inside the dictionary. Otherwise, authentication is rejected, as seen in the 2nd API request for the invalid_login_body. 

$ python3 authentication_test.py
Valid Login Response: Login successful
Valid login: Logged out successfully
Invalid login with username 'MIenna' and password 'wrongpassword' returned response: Invalid credentials

Authorisation

Definition:
Authorisation determines what an authenticated user is allowed to do. In Flask, this can be managed by defining roles and permissions.

Explanation:
This example demonstrates authorisation by checking a user's role before allowing access to certain resources. Only users with the "admin" role can access the admin page.

Below is a code snippet that authenticates users based on their roles and authorizes access accordingly. Both users admin and user1 is successfully authenticated, but the /admin API checks for admin permissions and denies access to user1, as they do not have the required permissions. 

$ python3 authorisation_test.py
Admin Login Response: Login successful
Admin Access to admin page: Welcome to the admin page
--------------------------------------------------
User1 Login Response: Login successful
User1 Access to admin page: Access denied

Accountability

Definition:
Accountability ensures that actions can be traced back to the responsible user. This is often implemented through logging user actions.

Explanation:
This example demonstrates accountability by logging user actions. Each action performed by a user is recorded in a log file, which can be reviewed to track user behaviour and ensure accountability.

The code below tests whether user actions are logged when a request is made to the /action API. The actions are recorded in the app.log file, as shown below.

WARNING:werkzeug: * Debugger is active!
INFO:werkzeug: * Debugger PIN: 579-674-550
INFO:root:User anonymous performed action: anonymous action
INFO:werkzeug:127.0.0.1 - - [22/Oct/2024 15:51:45] "POST /action HTTP/1.1" 200 -
INFO:root:User anonymous performed action: logged-in action
INFO:werkzeug:127.0.0.1 - - [22/Oct/2024 15:51:45] "POST /action HTTP/1.1" 200 -

1.5 Security Features

Syllabus
Apply security features incorporated into software, including data protection, security, privacy and regulatory compliance.

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand how to apply security features in software to ensure data protection, privacy, and regulatory compliance.
  • Learn to implement security features in software applications using best practices.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to explain the importance of data protection, security, privacy, and regulatory compliance in software development.
  • Students will be able to implement these security features in a software application.

  Content

Incorporating security features into software development is essential for safeguarding data, ensuring privacy, and adhering to regulatory requirements. These features are critical for preventing vulnerabilities, defending against attacks, and maintaining user trust. Below is an explanation of key aspects of data protection:

 

Data Protection

Data Protection

Data protection is a comprehensive approach to safeguarding data from vulnerabilities and unauthorised access while ensuring its confidentiality, integrity, and availability. It involves implementing various security measures to protect data throughout its lifecycle, whether stored, processed, or transmitted.

  • Encryption:
    Encrypt sensitive data at rest and in transit to prevent unauthorised access. Use strong encryption standards like AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) for stored data and TLS (Transport Layer Security) for data in transit.

  • Access Controls:
    Implement strict access controls to ensure only authorised users can access sensitive data. This may include role-based access control (RBAC), where users are granted access based on their organisational

  • Backups:
    Regularly back up data to secure locations to prevent data loss due to accidental deletion, corruption, or attacks like ransomware.

Example:

 

   Explanation

    • Encryption Process: The Fernet class from the cryptography Library is used to handle encryption and decryption. A key is generated when the application starts, which is then used to encrypt any data submitted to the /store_data endpoint.
    • Storing Data: When a user sends data to be stored, it is first encrypted using this key. This means that if someone were to gain unauthorised access to the stored data, it would appear as unreadable ciphertext.
    • Retrieving Data: The /retrieve_data endpoint allows you to decrypt the previously stored data. Only someone with access to the encryption key can decrypt the data, ensuring that sensitive information remains secure.

    This setup demonstrates how to protect data at rest by ensuring it is encrypted before being stored, thus preventing unauthorised.

 

Security

Security

Software security is designed to protect users from threats from unauthorised parties, ensuring their data and interactions with the software remain safe and secure. This involves implementing various security measures, such as authentication, encryption, access controls, and regular security assessments, to safeguard against potential threats.

  • Authentication and Authorisation: Verifying the user's identity when attempting to access a system. Strong authentication includes:
      • Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires providing two or more verification factors (or tokens) to gain access to a resource.
      • Strong Passwords - enforcing character restrictions or number requirements on passwords during registration. 
      •  Authorisation or authorisation to access specific resources. 
      • Roles-Based (RBAC) - assigning permissions to users based on roles within an organisation as teacher and student)
      • Access Control List - specifying which users or systems are granted permissions. For example, a file might have an ACL that specifies read, write, and execute permissions. 
  • Input Validation: Validating user-provided data is correct, safe and secure before processing, helping protect software from attacks (SQL injections, cross-site scripting and buffer overflows. To prevent this:
      • Sanitisation input must be provided on both the client and server sides.
      • Define acceptable input formats (allowing numbers only in a phone number field)
  • Security Audits: Systematically review the software, its environment, and its processes to ensure compliance with security policies, identify potential vulnerabilities, and verify the effectiveness of security measures. Audits can be performed internally by an organisation or by third-party auditors. 

Example:

 

   Explanation:

  • Password Hashing: When storing passwords, they are hashed using generate_password_hash, which ensures that even if someone gains access to the password database, they cannot retrieve the original passwords.
  • Authentication: When a user attempts to log in, the entered password is hashed and compared to the stored hash. If they match, the user is authenticated, and a session is created to maintain their login state.
  • Role-Based Access: The application checks the user's role status in the session to determine if they have permission to access certain resources. For example, only users with the "admin" role can"access" the /admin_resource endpoint.

This setup ensures that only authorised users can access sensitive areas of the application, protecting against unauthorised users.

 

Privacy

Privacy

Privacy in secure software protects an individual's personal data and information. 

  • Data minimisation is a concise database that stores only what is necessary to prevent privacy breaches. 
  • User Consent: Obtaining a user from the user client of obtaining permissions before collecting or processing data. Creating UI that has buttons or checkboxes for a consent form. 
  • Data Access Controls: Ensure that only authorised personnel can access private information—authorisation only for specific roles will access private data using a roles-based authorisation system.  

Example:

 

   Explanation:

  • Data Minimisation: The application only stores essential information, such as the user's email, to the user's risk of storing unnecessary personal data.
  • User Control: Users can delete their data from the system, allowing them to exercise control over their personal information, a core principle of privacy.

This setup exemplifies respecting user privacy by minimising data stored and giving users the power to manage their information.

 

Regulatory Compliance

Regulatory Compliance

Achieving regulatory compliance means aligning with legal and regulatory guidelines applicable to the region. Software developers must ensure that the software meets legal obligations and protects user data. 

  • Compliance Audits:
    Regularly conduct audits to ensure that the software complies with relevant regulations. This may include reviewing data handling practices, security measures, and user consent mechanisms.

  • Data Retention Policies:
    Implement data retention policies that comply with regulations, specifying how long data is stored and when it should be deleted.

  • User Consent:
    Ensure users consent before their data is collected, processed, or shared. This is especially important for sensitive personal data.

Example:

 

   Explanation:

  • User Consent: The application ensures that users have explicit consent before processing data. If a user does not consent, the action is denied.
  • Compliance Audits: The application includes a basic compliance audit that checks whether all users have provided the necessary consent. This is important for adhering to regulatory requirements such as GDPR, which mandates explicit user consent for data processing.

Content

Secure Software Architecture

This cycle delves deeper into the technical implementation of secure software systems. Moving beyond the foundational concepts, we explore how to proactively build security and privacy directly into software architecture from the ground up.

Throughout this cycle, we will cover the following key areas:

  • The 'Security by Design' approach, focusing on the technical pillars of cryptography and sandboxing.
  • Implementing the 'Privacy by Design' framework to ensure user data is proactively protected and respected.
  • Testing software resilience, determining vulnerabilities, handling breaches, and planning for business continuity and disaster recovery.
  • Utilising vital developer strategies and tools, including SAST, DAST, code reviews, and penetration testing.
  • Designing defensive code with robust data input handling, validation, and sanitisation to prevent malicious exploits like SQL injection.

Developing Secure Code

1.6 Security by Design

Syllabus
Use and explain the contribution of cryptography and sandboxing to the 'security by design' approach in the development of software solutions.

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the roles of cryptography and sandboxing in enhancing software security.
  • Learn how these techniques contribute to software development's' security by design' approach.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to explain the principles of cryptography and sandboxing.
  • Students will understand how these techniques are applied to improve software security.
  • Students will be able to incorporate cryptography and sandboxing into software development practices.

  Content

 

Using Cryptography and Sandboxing in 'Security by Design'

The 'security by design' approach involves integrating security measures into the software development process rather than adding them as an afterthought. Cryptography and sandboxing are two critical components of this approach, which significantly protect software from various threats.

 

Cryptography

   Definition

Cryptography is securing information by transforming it into an unreadable format, which can only be deciphered by those with the correct key. This technique is essential for protecting sensitive data and ensuring its confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity.

Contribution to 'Security by Design':

  • Confidentiality: Cryptography ensures that sensitive information remains private by encrypting data to only be accessible to authorised users. This is crucial in preventing data breaches and unauthorised access.
  • Integrity: Cryptographic techniques such as hashing verify that data has not been altered during transmission or storage, thus maintaining its integrity.
  • Authentication: Cryptography is used in authentication processes to verify the identities of users and devices, ensuring that only authorised parties can access the system.
  • Non-repudiation: Digital signatures, a form of cryptographic evidence, provide proof of the origin and integrity of data, preventing parties from denying their actions.

Example

  • Encryption: In this Flask application, cryptography encrypts data before storing or transmitting it. The data is converted into an unreadable format using a key required for decryption.
  • Decryption: When the data needs to be accessed, it is decrypted using the same key, converting it back into its original readable format. This ensures that sensitive information remains secure throughout its lifecycle.

Sandboxing

   Definition

Sandboxing is a security mechanism that isolates running programs or processes, limiting their access to the system and preventing them from making permanent changes. This technique executes untrusted code safely without risking the entire system's security.

 

Contribution to 'Security by Design':

  • Isolation: By isolating applications or processes in a sandbox, developers can prevent potential threats from spreading to the rest of the system. This containment reduces the risk of malware infections and system breaches.
  • Testing: Sandboxing allows developers to test new or untrusted code in a controlled environment. Any malicious behaviour or unexpected outcomes are contained within the sandbox, protecting the main system.
  • Mitigating Risks: Even if an application or process within a sandbox is compromised, the impact is limited to the sandboxed environment, thereby reducing the overall security risk.

Example

In software development, sandboxing is often used during testing to run potentially harmful code or untrusted applications without affecting the production environment. It ensures that the damage is contained even if the code has vulnerabilities.

  • Sandboxing Execution: In this example, the Flask application accepts code from the user and runs it in a sandboxed environment using the subprocess module. The code is executed with restricted permissions and a timeout, ensuring it does not affect the main system.
  • Controlled Environment: If the code contains harmful instructions or behaves unexpectedly, the damage is contained within the sandbox. This approach allows developers to test untrusted code securely without compromising the overall system's security.

1.7 Privacy by Design

Syllabus
Use and explain the 'privacy by design' approach in the development of software solutions, including: 
- proactive not reactive approach
- embed privacy into design
- respect for user privacy

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the core principles of software development's‘ privacy by design' approach.
  • Learn how to implement privacy-first practices throughout the software development lifecycle.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to explain the key principles of 'privacy by design'.
  • Students will be able to integrate privacy-focused features into software solutions.
  • Students will respect user privacy by embedding it directly into the software design.

  Content

 The 'privacy by design' approach means that privacy considerations are incorporated from the beginning of the software development process. It's not an afterthought but rather a proactive and essential part of the design process to safeguard user privacy throughout the software's lifecycle.

The three main principles of privacy by design are:

  • Proactive, not reactive approach
  • Embed privacy into design
  • Respect for user privacy

Each plays a crucial role in protecting users' personal information and complying with privacy regulations.

Proactive not reactive approach

   Definition

A proactive approach ensures that potential privacy issues are addressed before they occur. Instead of reacting to privacy breaches after they happen, developers anticipate and mitigate risks early in the design process.

 

Privacy by design is not reactive to privacy risks that materialise or occur. Instead, it is proactive by aiming to prevent any privacy threats from occurring. In the initial stages of the software development cycle, privacy impact assessments (PIAs) are conducted to identify and evaluate potential risks.



Developers will ensure the software design addresses these privacy issues proactively - where privacy protections are embedded into the software architecture and design before deployment.

How It Works:

  • Risk Assessment:
    Conduct privacy risk assessments during the planning and design stages to identify potential vulnerabilities and mitigate them before deployment.

  • Prevention Over Detection:
    Build privacy features that prevent issues rather than relying solely on detection mechanisms. This means implementing measures like anonymising data, minimising data collection, and encrypting sensitive information.

Example in Software Development:

A proactive approach would involve setting up privacy controls like consent mechanisms and data anonymisation during the project's initial stages and ensuring that these are embedded before the software is even deployed.

Embed privacy into design

   Definition

Embedding privacy into the design means that privacy measures are integrated directly into thesoftware'ss architecture, ensuring privacy is considered at every step of the development process. Privacy considerations should be incorporated into the core design and the software architecture. Privacy by design should include systematic embedding of privacy, data minimisation and encryption techniques to protect user privacy. 

How It Works:

  • Privacy as a Default:
    Systems should be designed with privacy features enabled by default. Users should not have to take extra steps to protect their privacy—it should be built into the system.

  • Minimal Data Collection:
    Limit the amount of personal data collected to the minimum required for the software to function, reducing the risk of data exposure.

Example in Software Development:

During the design phase, developers should ensure that all features respect user privacy by limiting data collection and securing stored data.



 

Respect for user privacy

   Definition

Respecting user privacy means giving users control over their data and ensuring transparency in handling their data. Users should be informed about what data is being collected and how it will be used, and they should be given options to manage or delete their information.

 

Respect for User Privacy aims to prioritise the interests and needs of individual users as the centre of Privacy by Design and is user-centric. The goal is to ensure that users have an active role in managing their data. 

This includes providing unambiguous consent to the use of private data. User Privacy should also be respected by limiting user data sharing with external third parties, ensuring confidentiality. 

How It Works:

  • User Control:
    Provide users with options to edit, delete, or export their information to manage their data. This shows respect for their ownership of the data.

  • Transparency:
    Clearly communicate with users about how their data is being used. Implement privacy policies that explain data practices in simple, understandable language.

Example in Software Development:

Incorporating user controls and transparency into the application's interface allows users to manage their personal information easily.

1.8 Test Security & Resilience

Syllabus
Test and evaluate the security and resilience of software by determining vulnerabilities, hardening systems, handling breaches, maintaining business continuity and conducting disaster recovery

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the core principles of software development's ‘privacy by design’ approach.
  • Learn how to implement privacy-first practices throughout the software development lifecycle.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to explain the key principles of ‘privacy by design’.
  • Students will be able to integrate privacy-focused features into software solutions.
  • Students will respect user privacy by embedding it directly into the software design.

  Content

Testing and evaluating software security and resilience ensures systems remain robust against attacks, can handle security breaches effectively, and recover quickly to maintain business continuity. This process involves determining vulnerabilities, hardening systems, handling breaches, and implementing disaster recovery plans.

 

Determining Vulnerabilities

   Definition

Vulnerabilities are weaknesses in software that attackers can exploit. Identifying and addressing these vulnerabilities is critical for building secure software.

How Vulnerabilities Are Addressed:

  • Penetration Testing (Pen Testing):
    Penetration testing involves ethical hackers attempting to exploit system weaknesses to identify potential vulnerabilities before attackers do.

  • Automated Vulnerability Scanning:
    Tools like Nessus and Qualys are used to scan systems for known vulnerabilities, comparing the system against databases of known security issues.

  • Code Audits and Reviews:
    Regular manual code reviews ensure secure coding practices and help identify weaknesses such as input validation issues or improper access control.

Example:
Financial institutions continuously automate vulnerability scanning to detect flaws in their infrastructure. They supplement this with periodic penetration testing by security specialists who simulate real-world attack scenarios, allowing the organisation to discover and fix vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

Hardening Systems

   Definition

Hardening involves securing a system by reducing its potential attack surface. This is achieved by limiting services, closing unused ports, and enforcing strict security policies.

How Systems Are Hardened:

  • Minimising Attack Surface:
    Disable or remove unnecessary services, applications, and features to reduce the points of entry for attackers.

  • Regular Patching and Updates:
    Systems are regularly updated with security patches to fix vulnerabilities. In industries like healthcare, maintaining updated systems is often a regulatory requirement.

  • Configuration Management:
    Secure configurations are enforced across systems using tools like Chef, Puppet, or Ansible, ensuring all systems are hardened with uniform security policies.

Example:
A global tech company enforces strict access control policies and regularly patches its systems using automated tools to ensure no known vulnerabilities are left unpatched. They also apply least-privilege access controls, ensuring users can only access the data and systems necessary for their role.

Handling Breaches

   Definition

A security breach occurs when an attacker gains unauthorised access to a system. Effectively handling a breach involves detecting, containing, and mitigating the damage caused.

How Breaches Are Managed:

  • Incident Response Teams (IRTs):
    Organisations have dedicated teams trained to detect, contain, and mitigate security breaches. These teams follow incident response plans, which outline procedures for addressing breaches.

  • Containment and Mitigation:
    When a breach is detected, affected systems are isolated to prevent the attacker from moving laterally within the network. Mitigation involves fixing the exploited vulnerability and preventing further attacks.

  • Forensic Investigation:
    After containment, forensic investigators analyse logs and network traffic to determine how the breach occurred and what data was compromised.

Example:
In 2020, a leading tech company detected a breach where hackers accessed their internal systems. Their incident response team immediately isolated the compromised servers, preventing the attack from spreading further. A forensic investigation revealed how the attackers had entered through an unpatched vulnerability, prompting an immediate patch and policy update.

Maintaining Business Continuity

   Definition

Business continuity ensures that essential operations can continue despite system disruptions or breaches. The goal is to minimise downtime and maintain operational capability.

How Business Continuity Is Maintained:

  • Redundancy and Failover:
    Critical systems have backup or redundant systems that automatically take over in the event of a failure. Cloud-based failover systems ensure that if one server goes down, another seamlessly takes over.

  • Data Backups:
    Regular backups ensure that the organisation can restore its systems in case of a data loss. Cloud backups or offsite storage ensures that data is protected even if physical infrastructure is compromised.

  • Business Continuity Plans (BCPs):
    Companies create detailed business continuity plans that outline how to maintain operations during a system outage or attack. These plans include steps for failover, key personnel assignments, and system recovery.

Example:
An e-commerce platform that operates globally uses a failover system to switch traffic between data centres in case one fails. By routing traffic through other servers, the company ensures minimal downtime, maintaining the ability for customers to make purchases during system maintenance or failure.

Conducting Disaster Recovery

   Definition

Disaster recovery focuses on restoring systems after a significant event, such as a security breach or natural disaster. The aim is to recover quickly and minimise long-term impact.

 

How Disaster Recovery Is Conducted:

  • Disaster Recovery Plans (DRPs):
    A Disaster Recovery Plan includes the steps needed to restore critical systems and services. This involves prioritising which systems to restore and ensuring resources are in place for recovery.

  • Backup Restoration:
    Regularly testing the restoration of backups ensures that backups are reliable and can be used in the event of data loss or system failure. Offsite or cloud backups are commonly used for redundancy.

  • Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO):
    Organisations set goals for how quickly services must be restored (RTO) and how much data loss is acceptable (RPO). These metrics help define recovery processes and ensure that critical services are restored within acceptable timeframes.

Example:
A bank that stores financial transactions in real-time performs regular disaster recovery drills to ensure it can restore operations within minutes of a failure. Data is mirrored across multiple servers, ensuring that the most recent transactions can be recovered and no critical data is lost.

1.9 Security Strategies & Tools

Syllabus
Apply and evaluate strategies used by software developers to manage the security of programming code: 
- code review
- static application security testing (SAST)
- dynamic application security testing (DAST)
- vulnerability assessment
- penetration testing

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the strategies software developers use to manage and improve the security of programming code.
  • Learn about the various testing methods and assessments used to identify and address security vulnerabilities in code.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Students will be able to explain different strategies used to evaluate and secure programming code.
  • Students will understand how to identify security flaws by applying code reviews, static and dynamic testing, vulnerability assessments, and penetration testing.
  • Students will evaluate the effectiveness of these strategies in real-world software development.

  Content

Code review

Sources of Error

Often, as programmers, we overlook errors within the code we write. This can stem from any number of reasons. Personal bias may be up there, and it is the same with negligence, but a far more frequent source of such errors comes from our understanding. We understand this code and believe it's the best way to do this specific task because we wrote it. We often don't see a need to question or refine our approach, not because of ego, but simply because we don't spare any more thought to our ideas and how we implement

 

The idea is that when a programmer needs to debug their code, they should explain the program line-by-line to a rubber duck. This results in a greater depth of code analysis and can help identify problem areas or find better approaches to issues. If your code is errored and you feel stuck, this might be one way to think through your problem rationally. And don't worry; you don't need a don't duck for this; it's purely metaphoricit'sYou can explain your code to any object, toy, dog, cat, or some fancy esoteric pet you might have around, or even.

As incredible as chatting to a rubber duck about your code may sound, it doesn't precisely. And, of course, the duck can't exactly talk, meaning you're stuck with your thoughts throughout the process. Sure, the thoughts might be more organised, but that doesn't always help; it's fresh out of you and doesn't account for sources of mistakes, bias and overconfidence, for example.

That's why we are involved in the process! Another person can bring a fresh perspective to your code and, this time around, even voice it. Of course, it's better if they are themselves programmers, even better if they have more knowledge to share, and even better if they are part of your team.

Professional Setting

If you are in a professional setting, or specifically in an experienced team, running your code by others to identify errors or mistakes is called a Code Review.

This has several aspects to it, though most organisations will have this as a last 'sanity check' before the code is deployed or added to the project but after the bots and testing software have had their way with it (we will cover these in the following sections), though some may place it before. Generally, these are done in the text through comments, as nobody has the time to hold a meeting after every change of code, but everyone has time to write up a couple of lines of text about some error they found while glancing the code over.

This is a more formal process than you may be used to. The scale of the professional software environment is much greater than the one you typically study in, with large teams cooperating on larger projects. So, let's run through an example code review in the developer platform you should all be familiar with at this point: GitHub.

 

Static application security testing (SAST)

Testing Software

We can have our digital tools check our code for us. They won’t be perfect either, as they can only do what we taught them to do. But they are accurate and can be relied on to do a job a relatively infinite amount of times without fail, which isn’t the case with people. As we saw prior, these are generally run after code is deemed “completed” by the programmer but can be run at any stage of development to ensure you’re on the right track.

Now, let’s look at our first digital Method of Testing.

 

SAST

Passive. That’s generally what the Static in the name represents. The defining characteristic of this testing method is that it looks through your code without running it.

The software used here is the programming equivalent of Microsoft Word Spellcheck. It looks through your code and tries to find possible issues and flaws based on information and patterns it has in its database. Generally, these are common flaws previously identified and added in. Much like our beloved Spellcheck holds a dictionary of words and checks grammar based on them, a SAST tool holds a dictionary of vulnerability patterns, meaning it works a bit in reverse, checking that none of these unsafe practices and patterns are within the code you give it. It then generates a report of its findings and recommendations for improving your code.

Let’s make an analogy that will help us contrast this methodology with another one later on. A SAST tool sits on the couch until you come and give it code to review. It takes out a highlighter and, still on the couch, circles everything you got wrong. It returns it to you, tells you what you should do, and keeps you sitting on the couch.

If that sounds a bit dull… It is, but there are two reasons. Firstly, it’s one-half of two methodologies used together, so hold your breath. Secondly, SAST tools are handy since they are pretty fast and tell you if you’re on the right track without using too much time or resources.

Bandit is a tool for performing Static Application Security Testing (SAST) on Python code, including Flask applications. By integrating Bandit into your development workflow, you can proactively identify and remediate security vulnerabilities early in the coding process, enhancing the overall security posture of your application.

Dynamic application security testing (DAST)

DAST is a black-box testing method that evaluates an application's security while running. It simulates external attacks on the application to identify vulnerabilities that attackers could exploit.

How DAST Works:

  • Testing in a Live Environment:
    DAST tools simulate attacks on the running application by sending inputs, such as malformed requests or known attack patterns, to see how the application responds.

  • Common Tools:
    Tools like OWASP ZAP (Zed Attack Proxy) and Burp Suite perform DAST by identifying security issues such as cross-site scripting (XSS), insecure authentication mechanisms, and weak session management.

 

Vulnerability assessment

The Vulnerability Assessment process, a comprehensive approach to system security, involves identifying, quantifying, and prioritising vulnerabilities within a system. Programmers are responsible for ensuring the system's security by conducting checks before sending the code for review or production. This assessment entails a thorough analysis and documentation, typically a checklist of items to be reviewed and verified, ensuring robust system security.

In an extensive application, the process generally includes the following steps:

1. Identifying possible vulnerabilities.
2. Analysing the findings to determine potential issues and risks associated with the identified vulnerabilities.
3. Perform a risk assessment to evaluate the likelihood and consequences of each risk and prioritise the risks for mitigation.
4. Remediation of the identified risks and vulnerabilities may involve removing vulnerabilities, managing risks in alternative ways, and establishing preventive measures or contingencies for potential risks.

Penetration testing

On the other hand, Penetration Testing involves simulating cyberattacks to evaluate a system's security. It is an authorised attempt to breach Penetration testing, often called "pen testing," which simulates real-world cyberattacks to identify security vulnerabilities that malicious actors could exploit. Pen testing helps determine an application's security posture by actively attempting to breach its defences.

How Penetration Testing Works:

  • Simulated Attacks:
    Ethical hackers (pen testers) use various methods to exploit known and unknown vulnerabilities in a system. This can include attempting to bypass authentication, gain access to sensitive data, or escalate privileges.

  • Manual and Automated Approaches:
    Pen testers use automated tools and manual techniques to simulate realistic attacks. Tools like Metasploit and Kali Linux are often used alongside manual methods to perform penetration tests.

This process typically follows a five-step approach:

1. Planning and reconnaissance: Gathering information about the target system.
2. Scanning: Using tools to understand how the target system responds to various intrusion attempts.
3. Gaining Access: Attempting to exploit vulnerabilities to gain access to the system.
4. Maintaining Access: Trying to sustain access to achieve the test's goals while overcoming protective measures.
5. Analysis and Reporting: Compiling the results and providing recommendations based on the penetration test findings.

1.10 Defensive Data

Syllabus
•    Design, develop and implement code using defensive data input handling practices, including input validation, sanitisation and error handling

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand and implement defensive data input handling practices in software development.
  • Learn the principles of input validation, data sanitisation, and error handling to safeguard applications from vulnerabilities.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Correctly implement input validation to ensure user data adheres to the expected format.
  • Apply data sanitisation techniques to prevent malicious input from compromising the software.
  • Implement error-handling mechanisms that provide meaningful feedback while maintaining security.

  Content

In software development, ensuring that data input is handled securely is critical to maintaining the integrity and security of the system. Implementing defensive data input handling practices is essential to protecting the system from common attacks such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and other input-based vulnerabilities.

Input Validation

Input validation ensures that the data entered by users meets the expected format before it is processed or stored by the system. This is the first line of defence against invalid or malicious input.

  • Types of Validation:

    • Server-side Validation: This occurs on the server, validating the data after it has been sent to it. It is more secure but may introduce delays as it requires communication with the server.
    • Client-side Validation: Performed on the client (e.g., in the browser) before data is sent to the server. This improves user experience but can be bypassed, so it should never be the only validation step.

  • Examples of Input Validation:

    • Type Checking: Ensure the input is of the expected data type (e.g., a number, string, date). 
      if type(value) == int:
    • Length Checking: Restrict input data length (e.g., the string must be < 20).
      if len(string) < 20:
    • Range Checking: Validate that numerical inputs fall within an expected range (e.g., age must be between 0 and 120).
      if age >= 0 and age <= 120:
    • Mandatory Fields:  Ensure that required fields are not left blank.
      if not name:

Data Sanitisation 

Data sanitisation involves cleaning user input by removing or escaping characters that could be interpreted as executable code, thereby preventing malicious data from compromising the system.

  • Why it’s important: Untrusted input, if not properly sanitised, can lead to security vulnerabilities like SQL injection and XSS, where attackers can manipulate input to execute unintended commands.

  • Sanitisation Techniques:

    • Escaping characters: Replacing potentially dangerous characters (like <, >, ', etc.) with safe representations.
    • Whitelist-based filtering: Accepting only known good input (e.g., allowing only alphanumeric characters for usernames).
    • Converting Data Types: Command-line inputs are strings, and the code requires the type to be a number/integer for calculations. For example,
      age = input("Enter your age: ") # input is a string
      age = int(age) # Convert to integer for numerical operations 

Error Handling

Error handling is a critical practice that ensures that when unexpected input or issues occur, the system can respond gracefully without exposing sensitive information or crashing.

  • Principles of Secure Error Handling:

    • User-friendly messages: Provide generic error messages to the end-user that do not disclose sensitive system information.
    • Detailed logging: Record detailed error information for developers or system administrators to investigate while keeping this information hidden from the user.

  • Example: Handling an error when an invalid file format is uploaded could involve rejecting the upload, notifying the user of acceptable formats, and logging the specific technical error for debugging.

In Python, error-handling messages can be used with the print() function. These error statements help log errors and provide feedback to guide users in correcting their inputs. For example, print("Password must be at least 20 characters") .

Example of Defensive Data Input Handling in Python:

  • The is_valid_username function validates that the username is alphanumeric and between 5-15 characters.
  • The re.escape() method sanitises input by escaping special characters, preventing SQL injection or similar attacks.
  • Error handling is implemented to provide a generic message when the user accesses an invalid route, keeping the system secure while offering meaningful feedback.

Developing Secure Code: Advanced Implementation

In this cycle, we transition from the conceptual foundations of security to the practical implementation of secure code. We will examine the intricate details of application vulnerabilities and how to construct robust defences against sophisticated attacks.

This cycle focuses on the following crucial areas of software engineering:
