Testing and evaluating

4.21 Test and Evaluate Code

Syllabus

Apply methodologies to test and evaluate code

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • To understand and apply methodologies for testing and evaluating code in order to ensure its functionality, efficiency, and reliability.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Identify different testing methodologies used in software development.
  • Apply appropriate testing techniques to evaluate the performance and functionality of code.
  • Understand how to interpret test results to improve code quality.
  • Use debugging tools to identify and resolve issues in code.

  Content

Code testing is a critical process in software development aimed at ensuring that the code functions as intended, without bugs or errors. It involves various methodologies that test different aspects of the software, such as functionality, performance, and security.

 

Types of Testing

  • Manual Testing: Testing performed by a human without using automated tools. It is often used for exploratory testing or when dealing with complex scenarios that require human judgement.
  • Automated Testing: Tests that run automatically using scripts or testing software. This is more efficient for repetitive tasks and large-scale projects.

 

Common Testing Methodologies

Software testing is performed in various stages, each targeting different aspects of the code. These stages, or levels of testing, ensure that the software is thoroughly checked from the smallest units of code to the fully integrated system. Each level focuses on a specific part of the software, with the goal of identifying and resolving defects as early as possible in the development process.

The levels of testing include:

  1. Unit Testing – Testing individual components or functions of the code in isolation.
  2. Integration Testing – Ensuring that different modules work together correctly.
  3. System Testing – Verifying that the entire application functions as expected in its environment.
  4. Acceptance Testing – Confirming that the software meets the business requirements and is ready for deployment.

 

Unit Testing

Unit testing involves testing individual components (or units) of the software to ensure that each part works as expected. Typically, developers write unit tests to check specific functions or methods in isolation from the rest of the codebase.

  • Methodology: Write test cases for each function or method and execute them. If the function passes the test cases, it is considered functional.
  • Tools: JUnit (for Java), pytest (for Python).

Integration Testing

Integration testing evaluates how different units or modules of the software work together. The goal is to identify issues in the interaction between integrated components.

  • Methodology: Once unit testing is done, combine related modules and test them as a group to ensure they function correctly when integrated.
  • Tools: Selenium (for web applications), Postman (for API testing).

System Testing

System testing involves testing the complete and integrated software product to ensure that the application as a whole meets the specified requirements.

  • Methodology: Test the application in a real-world environment by running functional and non-functional tests (e.g., usability, performance). It usually comes after integration testing.
  • Tools: TestRail, Apache JMeter (for performance testing).

Acceptance Testing

Acceptance testing checks whether the software meets the business requirements and is ready for delivery to the customer. It is often carried out by the end-users or stakeholders.

  • Methodology: Create scenarios that mimic user behaviour to verify that the system operates as expected under typical usage.
  • Types: User Acceptance Testing (UAT), Operational Acceptance Testing (OAT).
  • Tools: Cucumber, Zephyr.

 

 

Test-Driven Development

Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a software development process where developers write tests before writing the code. This approach encourages designing small, testable units and focusing on ensuring that each part of the code passes the tests.

  • Methodology: Write a test for the new functionality -> Write the code -> Run the test (should fail initially) -> Refactor the code -> Run the test again (should pass).
  • Advantages: Helps in writing clean, bug-free code and provides a set of regression tests as a by-product.
  • Tools: JUnit, NUnit, pytest.

 

Debugging and Error Handling

Testing helps identify issues, but debugging is the process of locating the cause of an error and fixing it.

  • Debugging Tools: Integrated Development Environments (IDEs) like Visual Studio or IntelliJ IDEA provide built-in debuggers to step through code, monitor variables, and trace the origin of bugs.
  • Error Handling: Developers should also include proper error handling within the code, ensuring that unexpected conditions (e.g., invalid user input) are gracefully managed.

 

Evaluating Code Performance

In addition to functionality, it’s crucial to evaluate the performance of the code to ensure it is efficient. This can be done through performance testing, which assesses how well the software performs under stress, load, and various conditions.

Performance Evaluation Techniques:

  • Load Testing: Determines how the software behaves under expected user loads.
  • Stress Testing: Puts the software under extreme conditions to identify its breaking point.
  • Profiling: Identifies bottlenecks in the code that may be causing inefficiency.

4.22 Code Optimisation

Syllabus

Use a language-dependent code optimisation technique

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand the concept of code optimisation and recognise the importance of performance improvements in Python programs.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain what code optimisation is and why it's important.
  • Identify and apply a Python-specific code optimisation technique.
  • Utilise list comprehensions in Python and explain why they improve performance over traditional loops.

  Content

What is Code Optimisation? 

Code Optimisation is the process of improving the performance and efficiency of a program by making it run faster and consuming fewer computational resources. 

Optimisation can be approached in two main ways:

  1. Language-Independent Optimisation: Techniques like reducing algorithmic complexity, eliminating redundant code, or improving data structures can apply to almost any programming language.

  2. Language-Dependent Optimisation: Techniques using language-specific features to enhance performance. 
    For example, Python-specific constructs can make Python code more efficient.

 

Code Optimisation in Python

Recap: Python Peformance

Python is a high-level, interpreted language that executes code line by line rather than compiling it into machine code like C or C++. This makes it slower than compiled languages, which execute directly on hardware.

 Therefore, language-specific optimisation in Python is challenging.

However, as the Python interpreter is written in C, we can leverage many in-built functions implemented in C and optimised for performance. These built-in functions are generally faster than writing equivalent logic manually in Python.

 

1. Use Built-in Functions and Libraries

Python provides highly optimised built-in functions like sum(), max(), min(), sorted(), and map(), which are implemented in C and run significantly faster than manual loops.

▶ Video won't play offline. Watch on Canvas · all modules
https://codesandbox.io/p/devbox/zealous-sun-hx7vzv?embed=1&amp;file=%2Fmain.py

 

2. List Comprehension

In Python, a list comprehension is a concise way to create lists. It’s faster than using a traditional for loop to iterate through a list and apply some operation to each element. This performance boost is because list comprehensions are implemented as C loops internally in Python, making them more efficient than a standard Python loop.

Example 1: Traditional For Loop vs List Comprehension

Let’s say we want to create a list of squares of numbers from 0 to 9.

Using a traditional for loop:

 

Using a list comprehension:

Both pieces of code generate the same output: [0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81]

However, the list comprehension is more efficient regarding speed and memory usage. This is because the overhead of appending to a list in the traditional loop is eliminated in the list comprehension, where the entire operation happens internally at once.

Extension: timeit()

Try write Python code to compare the performance of a traditional for loop with a list comprehension using the timeit module. You will perform multiple trials and calculate the average execution time for both approaches.

Objective

  • Use the timeit() function to measure and compare the execution time of a for loop and a list comprehension.
  • Perform multiple trials to average the times and determine which approach is faster.

 

The timeit() function allows you to time small code snippets. Here’s what each parameter does:

  • stmt: The code you want to time as a string (e.g., "for i in range(10): pass").
  • setup: Optional. Any code that needs to run before timing begins (e.g., importing modules or initialising variables).
  • number: The number of times to run the code. More iterations will give a more stable average.

 

Example usage:

timeit.timeit(stmt="for i in range(10): pass", setup="", number=10000)

 

  • Run the trials and record the average times.
  • Compare the average times for the for loop and the list comprehension.
  • Which method was faster, and why do you think it performed better? 

 

Why is this Optimisation Effective in Python?

  1. Fewer Lines of Code: List comprehensions are more concise, which means fewer opportunities for errors and easier maintenance.
  2. Internal Optimisation: Python internally optimises list comprehensions using highly efficient C implementations.
  3. Better Memory Usage: Since list comprehensions are optimised for execution, they tend to use memory more efficiently, reducing the overhead of appending items in loops.

4.23 Feedback

Syllabus

Analyse and respond to feedback

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • To understand how to effectively analyse and respond to feedback in the context of software engineering, enhancing the quality and functionality of software products.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Identify different types of feedback relevant to software engineering.
  • Analyse feedback for actionable insights to improve software projects.
  • Develop strategies for incorporating constructive criticism into the development cycle.
  • Evaluate the impact of responding to feedback on project success and team dynamics.

  Content

Feedback is a critical component of the software development lifecycle. It provides developers, project managers, and other stakeholders with essential insights into how the software performs, whether it meets user requirements, and where improvements are needed. Effective feedback analysis ensures that projects evolve to meet user needs and maintain high standards of quality and performance.

 

Types of Feedback in Software Engineering:

In software engineering, feedback can be categorised into the following key types:

  1. User Feedback: This comes directly from end-users who interact with the software. It often relates to user experience (UX), usability, and functionality. Users may highlight bugs, suggest new features, or express difficulties in navigating the software.

  2. Stakeholder Feedback: Feedback from clients, project sponsors, and business stakeholders is crucial. It focuses on whether the software aligns with the project goals, meets business needs, and satisfies project constraints (such as time and budget).

  3. Peer or Team Feedback: Developers, testers, and other team members provide peer feedback during code reviews, sprint reviews, and collaborative problem-solving sessions. This type of feedback focuses on technical quality, code efficiency, and adherence to standards.

  4. Automated Feedback: Tools like Continuous Integration (CI) pipelines, static analysis tools, and automated testing frameworks generate feedback regarding code quality, performance, and reliability. These feedback mechanisms help catch issues early in the development process.

 

Analysing Feedback

The ability to critically evaluate feedback is essential to the success of a software project. The steps to analyse feedback include:

  1. Categorisation: Sort feedback based on its nature and origin (user, peer, stakeholder, or automated). This helps developers prioritise and handle feedback efficiently.

    • Example: User-reported bugs should be prioritised differently from automated performance warnings.

  2. Validity and Relevance: Not all feedback is equally valuable. Developers must assess whether feedback is relevant, aligns with the project’s goals, and is feasible to implement.

    • Example: A feature request that aligns with the project scope and user needs is more actionable than a request that falls outside the intended purpose of the software.

  3. Impact Analysis: Evaluate how implementing changes based on the feedback will affect the software, including its architecture, performance, or user satisfaction. Some changes may introduce new issues, requiring further adjustments.

    • Example: A user might suggest an interface change that improves usability but adds complexity to the codebase. The impact on both usability and technical debt should be considered.

  4. Urgency and Priority: Address high-priority feedback first. For example, critical bugs affecting software functionality or security take precedence over minor cosmetic issues.

Responding to Feedback

Once feedback has been analysed, it’s essential to act on it efficiently and transparently. The following strategies can guide the response:

  1. Incorporation into Agile Processes: In Agile software development, feedback is often gathered and incorporated during sprints. User stories, tasks, or bugs can be created based on feedback, ensuring it is formally included in the development cycle.

    • Example: A bug reported by a user during beta testing can be included as a task in the next sprint, ensuring it is addressed promptly.

  2. Communication: Keeping stakeholders and users informed about how their feedback is being handled builds trust and ensures alignment between developers and project goals.

    • Example: Regular updates during sprint reviews or feedback channels, such as forums or emails, allow users to see how their feedback has influenced development.

  3. Iterative Improvement: Responding to feedback should be an ongoing process. Iterating based on feedback during multiple development cycles helps improve software gradually.

    • Example: An initial release may receive feedback about performance issues. Subsequent releases should address these issues, and new feedback should guide further refinement.

  4. Balance Between New Features and Bug Fixes: It’s important to balance responding to feature requests with maintaining software stability. While new features may enhance user satisfaction, unresolved bugs or performance issues can degrade user experience.

    • Example: Implementing a new feature from user feedback is great, but not if it causes significant regressions or introduces critical bugs.

  5. Learning from Feedback: Feedback provides a valuable learning opportunity for developers. Constructive criticism from peers and code reviews can enhance technical skills, improve collaboration, and help ensure better design choices.

    • Example: If feedback identifies inefficient code patterns, the development team can use this to improve coding standards and ensure better performance in future iterations.

 

Callout Heading

  • Improved Software Quality: Timely and constructive feedback leads to a more polished, stable, and user-friendly product.
  • Increased User Satisfaction: Addressing user feedback fosters a sense of community and trust, ensuring that users feel heard and valued.
  • Enhanced Collaboration: Regular peer reviews and open feedback improve team collaboration and lead to better code quality.
  • Continuous Improvement: An iterative feedback-response loop ensures continuous software enhancement, avoiding stagnation and helping meet evolving user needs.

4.24 Effectiveness

Syllabus

Evaluate the effectiveness of a software engineering solution, including:

  • developing a report to synthesise feedback
  • developing a test plan
  • testing data used/generated based on path and boundary testing
  • comparing actual output with expected output

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • To evaluate the effectiveness of a software engineering solution by synthesising feedback, developing a test plan, applying path and boundary testing, and comparing actual versus expected outcomes.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Develop a structured report that synthesises feedback from stakeholders.
  • Create a comprehensive test plan covering all relevant scenarios.
  • Apply path and boundary testing techniques to evaluate software robustness.
  • Accurately compare actual output with expected output to assess the solution's performance.

  Content

An effective software evaluation begins by gathering feedback from a range of stakeholders. This feedback offers valuable insights into how the software performs from different perspectives, such as user experience, performance, and feature implementation.

Synthesising Feedback:

Once feedback is gathered, it must be synthesised into a clear, actionable report. The report should:

  1. Categorise feedback into relevant sections (e.g., user experience, performance, functionality).
  2. Prioritise feedback based on severity or frequency of issues. A common approach is to categorise issues as critical, high, medium, or low priority.
  3. Provide action items based on feedback, such as recommendations for further testing, redesign, or feature modification.
Effectiveness: Test Plan
Effectiveness Criteria:

  • Completeness: Includes all functional and non-functional requirements.

    • Effectiveness: Ensures no critical feature is left untested.

  • Accuracy & Reliability of Tests: Produce consistent and reproducible results?

    • Effectiveness: Prevents false positives/negatives, ensuring reliable test outcomes.

  • Testing Environment: 

    • Performance Testing: Stress, load, and performance testing?
      • Effectiveness: Ensures software stability under peak usage conditions.

    • Real-World Simulation: Replicates high traffic, concurrent users, and hardware variations.
      • Effectiveness: Confirms system resilience and scalability.

  • Test Execution Time & Resource Usage

    • Optimised Execution: Avoids redundant or slow-running tests.

      • Effectiveness: Speeds up testing without compromising coverage.

    • Resource Efficiency: Minimises CPU, memory, and network overhead.

      • Effectiveness: Prevents performance bottlenecks during testing cycles.
Effectiveness: Path Testing
Effectiveness Criteria: 

  • Test Coverage: Ensure all logical paths in the program are executed at least once.

    • Effectiveness: Detects missing logic, dead code, and untested execution flows.

  • Boundary Testing: Focuses on edge values rather than general inputs.

    • Effectiveness: Identifies off-by-one errors, overflow issues, and incorrect condition handling

  • Comprehensive Testing Data:

    • Effectiveness: Uses a mix of valid, invalid, extreme, and edge case inputs to test system reliability.
Effectiveness: Synthesis Report
Effectiveness Criteria: 

  • Accuracy of Feedback Aggregation: Collects, categorises, and summarises feedback

    • Effectiveness: Ensures feedback is grouped correctly without misclassification or data loss.

  • Relevance & Quality of Insights: Extracts key trends and actionable insights from feedback.

    • Effectiveness: Avoids generating overly generic or irrelevant summaries.

 

Developing a Test Plan

A test plan is essential for systematically evaluating the functionality, performance, and reliability of the software. The test plan should be comprehensive, covering all critical aspects of the solution.

Components of a Test Plan:

  • Scope: Clearly defines what features and functionalities are being tested, as well as any areas that will not be covered in this round of testing. This ensures focused and efficient testing.

  • Objectives: Outline what the testing seeks to achieve, such as verifying that the system meets performance benchmarks or that the user interface behaves correctly under different conditions.

  • Test cases: Individual scenarios to be tested, often based on user stories or specific functional requirements. Each test case should include:

    • Preconditions: The state of the system before the test is run.

    • Test data: Input values required to execute the test.

    • Steps: The sequence of actions to perform the test.

    • Expected outcome: What should happen when the test is executed.

    • Example: For a password reset feature, a test case might involve the following:

      • Precondition: The user must have an account.
      • Test data: Email address associated with the account.
      • Steps: Request password reset, enter email, receive reset link, enter new password.
      • Expected outcome: User is redirected to the login page, and the password reset email is successfully delivered.

  • Test environment: Specifies the hardware, software, and network configurations under which the tests will be executed, ensuring consistency and accuracy in results.

  • Test criteria: Define success or failure for each test case. For example, a pass might be logged if the system behaves exactly as described in the expected outcomes, while deviations would be logged as failures.

Path and Boundary Testing

Path testing and boundary testing are key techniques for ensuring that a software solution behaves correctly under various conditions.

Path Testing:

Path testing involves exploring the different execution paths within a software system to ensure that all logic flows and decision points are correctly implemented. This is particularly useful for condition-heavy code, such as authentication systems or decision-making algorithms.

  • How it works: In path testing, testers identify all possible paths a user might take through the software. For each path, they create test cases to ensure that every branch and conditional statement in the code is executed at least once.

    • Example: A payment system that checks for available funds, verifies the user's identity, and processes the payment must have tests for paths where the payment succeeds, paths where the payment fails due to insufficient funds, and paths where the user authentication fails.

Boundary Testing:

Boundary testing focuses on edge cases—the extreme ends of input values. These are often the points where software can fail due to overlooked assumptions or insufficient validation.

  • How it works: Testers design inputs that lie just inside and outside the boundary values of input ranges. By doing so, they assess how the software behaves when pushed to its limits.

    • Example: For a form field requiring a username between 5 and 15 characters, boundary tests would include:
      • Valid inputs: 5 characters, 15 characters.
      • Invalid inputs: 4 characters, 16 characters.

    Boundary testing is crucial in identifying issues like array overflows, incorrect validation, or performance degradation under extreme input conditions.

Comparing Actual Output with Expected Output

Once testing is complete, it’s essential to compare the actual output of the software with the expected output defined during the test planning phase. This step helps validate the correctness of the solution and identify discrepancies that indicate bugs or unmet requirements.

Key Comparison Steps:

  • Capture actual output: During the execution of test cases, record the system’s behaviour. This could involve logging error messages, system responses, database states, or interface behaviours.

  • Compare against expected outcomes: For each test case, the actual results are compared to the expected outcomes to verify correctness.

    • Example: For a login system:
      • Test case: User enters correct credentials.
      • Expected output: System redirects to the dashboard.
      • Actual output: If the user is instead redirected to an error page, there is a discrepancy that needs addressing.

  • Document discrepancies: If the actual and expected outcomes differ, document the details for further investigation. Each discrepancy should be classified according to its severity (e.g., critical, high, medium, low) and assigned to a development team for resolution.

Regression Testing:

If fixes are applied, it’s important to conduct regression testing to ensure that the changes do not introduce new issues elsewhere in the software. This process involves re-running relevant test cases to verify the integrity of the overall system after modifications.

3.7 Regression Models

Syllabus

Design, develop and apply ML regression models using an OOP to predict numeric values, including:

  • linear regression
  • polynomial regression
  • logistic regression

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Design, develop, and implement machine learning regression models using an object-oriented programming (OOP) approach to predict numeric values, including linear regression, polynomial regression, and logistic regression.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain the differences between linear, polynomial, and logistic regression.
  • Design classes in Python to represent regression models, using inheritance and encapsulation effectively.
  • Implement OOP-based regression models to solve prediction tasks and assess their performance using appropriate metrics.

  Content

Regression models are essential tools in machine learning for predicting numerical values based on input data. In this lesson, we explore the development and application of three key regression models—linear regression, polynomial regression, and logistic regression—using an object-oriented programming (OOP) approach. By adopting OOP principles, we can design flexible and reusable models that efficiently handle different types of prediction tasks.

Linear regression helps in modelling relationships between variables through a straight line, while polynomial regression extends this to capture more complex, non-linear relationships. Logistic regression, though commonly associated with classification, is included here to highlight its use in predicting probabilities for binary outcomes. Through these models, you will gain a deeper understanding of how to apply regression techniques to solve real-world problems in a structured, scalable manner.

 

Why use OOP to design models?

Traditionally, regression models can be written in procedural or declarative. However, using OOP, developers can create scalable regression models! This means we can leverage powerful OOP features, including:

  • Scalability – Easily extend models with inheritance.
  • Modularity – Keep data and logic together with encapsulation.
  • Maintainability – Enforce structured models with abstraction.
  • Flexibility – Swap different regression models dynamically using polymorphism.

 

Linear Regression

Linear regression is a supervised learning algorithm that models the relationship between a dependent variable (target) and one or more independent variables (features) by fitting a linear equation to observed data.

Key Equation:

y=β0+β1x1+β2x2+⋯+βnxn+ϵy = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots + \beta_n x_n + \epsilon

Where:

  • yy is the predicted output (dependent variable).
  • x1,x2,…,xnx_1, x_2, \dots, x_n are the input features (independent variables).
  • β0\beta_0 is the intercept, and β1,…,βn\beta_1, \dots, \beta_n​ are the coefficients (slopes) of the model.
  • ϵ\epsilon represents the error term (residuals).

 

Basic Structure for Defining a LinearRegression Class:

  • Attributes: Coefficients, intercept, learning rate, number of iterations.
  • Methods:
    • fit(): Trains the model by calculating optimal coefficients using gradient descent.
    • predict(): Uses the fitted model to predict values for new data.
    • evaluate(): Calculates performance metrics such as Mean Squared Error (MSE).

 

Applications:

  • Predicting housing prices based on features like square footage, number of bedrooms, etc.
  • Forecasting sales figures based on past data.

Polynomial Regression

Polynomial regression is an extension of linear regression where the relationship between the input variables and output is modelled as an nth-degree polynomial.

Key Equation:

y=β0+β1x+β2x2+⋯+βnxn+ϵy = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \dots + \beta_n x^n + \epsilon

  • The model is still linear in terms of the coefficients, but the features are transformed into polynomial terms.

Basic Structure to Implement Polynomial Regression in OOP:

    • Inherit from LinearRegression to reuse logic for fitting and prediction.
    • Additional Attribute: Degree of the polynomial.
    • Method: transform() that converts input features into polynomial terms.

 

Applications:

  • Modelling non-linear relationships, such as growth curves or natural phenomena like temperature variation.

Logistic Regression

Although its name includes "regression," logistic regression is used for binary classification tasks. It predicts the probability of a binary outcome (e.g., yes/no, 0/1).

Key Equation:

p(x)=11+e−(β0+β1x1+⋯+βnxn)p(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_n x_n)

Where:

  • p(x)p(x is the predicted probability.
  • The model uses the sigmoid function to map predictions to a range between 0 and 1.

Basic Structure to Implement Logistic Regression in OOP:

    • Inherit from LinearRegression.
    • Methods: Implement the sigmoid activation and adjust the gradient descent to minimise the cross-entropy loss instead of MSE.

 

Applications:

  • Classifying whether a customer will purchase a product (yes/no).
  • Predicting whether a patient has a disease (0/1).

 

MODEL TYPE TASK TYPE
 EQUATION TYPE USE CASES
Linear Regression Predicting continuous values Linear equation Housing prices, stock predictions
Polynomial Regression
 Predicting continuous values Polynomial equation Growth modelling, complex non-linear phenomena
Logistic Regression
 Binary classification Sigmoid Binary outcomes like spam detection, diagnosis

3.8 Predictions with Neural Network Models

Syllabus

Apply neural network models using an OOP to make predictions

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Apply neural network models using an object-oriented programming (OOP) approach to make predictions by building and training simple feedforward neural networks.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain the structure and functioning of a neural network.
  • Design a neural network model class using OOP principles.
  • Implement a basic neural network to perform prediction tasks and assess its performance.

  Content

Neural networks are powerful machine learning algorithms inspired by the structure of the human brain, designed to recognise complex patterns in data. By using an object-oriented programming (OOP) approach, we can create flexible and reusable neural network models to solve prediction tasks effectively.

Neural networks, particularly feedforward neural networks, consist of layers of interconnected nodes (neurons). These models are especially useful when dealing with large datasets with complex relationships that traditional regression models might struggle to capture.

 

Recall: Key Concepts of Neural Networks

  • Neurons and Layers:

    • A neural network consists of an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer. Each neuron in a layer receives inputs, applies weights and biases, and passes the result through an activation function to produce an output.

  • Feedforward Process:

    • In a feedforward neural network, data flows in one direction—from the input layer, through hidden layers, and to the output layer—without loops or cycles.

  • Activation Function:

    • The activation function introduces non-linearity to the model, enabling the network to learn and model complex relationships. Common activation functions include ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) and sigmoid.

  • Backpropagation and Gradient Descent:

    • Neural networks are trained using backpropagation, a method that calculates the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight in the network. This information is used to update the weights through gradient descent.

 

Implementing a Neural Network Using OOP

To build a neural network, we'll use OOP principles, creating a class-based design that encapsulates the functionality of a neural network and its training process. The structure of the class will allow for flexibility in modifying the network's architecture and training process.

 

Class Structure

A key benefit of OOP is the ability to encapsulate the functionality of the neural network into a single class. This class can manage the network's architecture (layers, neurons, weights, and biases), the forward and backward passes, and the training loop. Think of the class as the "blueprint" for how the neural network behaves.

Attributes:

In the neural network class, the attributes will store the essential information about the network:

  • Layers: Define the architecture of the neural network (e.g., input layer, hidden layers, output layer).
  • Weights and Biases: Initialise random weights and biases for the connections between neurons in different layers.
  • Learning Rate: Controls how much the model's weights are updated with respect to the error gradient during training.

Example class initialisation:

 

 

Weight Initialisation:

Neural networks rely on weights and biases to adjust their predictions during training. These are initialised randomly at first.

Each connection between neurons in different layers gets a corresponding weight and bias.

Feedforward Process

The feedforward process computes the output of the neural network by passing the input data through each layer, applying weights, biases, and an activation function. This process is central to how neural networks make predictions.

How it Works:

  • Multiply the input by the weights, add the bias, and apply an activation function to introduce non-linearity. Popular activation functions include ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) and sigmoid.

In code, the forward pass might look like this:

The a_values variable stores the activations at each layer, which are passed through the network.

 

As neural networks involve multiple layers and complex transformations, the forward pass can be thought of like a journey: the input data gets progressively transformed through each layer until it reaches the output.

Activation Function

An activation function is essential in neural networks to introduce non-linearity, allowing the network to learn complex patterns. Without it, the model would simply perform linear transformations and wouldn't be able to solve complex tasks.

Popular choices:

  • ReLU: f(z)=max⁡(0,z)f(z) = \max(0, z)
  • Sigmoid: f(z)=11+e−zf(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}

Think of the activation function like a "filter" that lets the network make more nuanced decisions, much like how our brain processes subtle details. The activation function, by allowing non-linearity, gives the machine a form of intelligence to handle complex problems.

Backpropagation

Backpropagation is the heart of neural network training. It calculates the gradient of the loss function with respect to each weight using the chain rule of calculus, allowing the network to update its weights to minimise the prediction error.

How it Works:

  • During backpropagation, the network compares its output to the actual target (label) and computes the error (using a loss function like mean squared error for regression or cross-entropy for classification).
  • The network then "propagates" this error backward through the layers, calculating how much each weight contributed to the error.

 

 

The backward() method adjusts the weights and biases according to the gradients to minimise the error. Just as in life, where we learn from our mistakes, the network adjusts its internal parameters based on the errors it encounters.

Training

The train() method loops through the data, performs forward and backward passes, and updates the weights. This is where the network actually learns.

Training involves multiple iterations (epochs) over the dataset. With each iteration, the model’s predictions improve as the weights are refined.

3.9 Impact of Automation

Syllabus

Assess the impact of automation on the individual, society and the environment, including:

  • safety of workers
  • people with disability
  • the nature and skills required for employment
  • production efficiency, waste and the environment
  • the economy and distribution of wealth

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Assess the impact of automation on individuals, society, and the environment, particularly in terms of worker safety, inclusivity for people with disabilities, employment skills, production efficiency, and economic disparities.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain how automation affects worker safety and people with disabilities.
  • Evaluate how automation changes the nature of work and the skills required for employment.
  • Assess the effects of automation on production efficiency, waste, and environmental sustainability.
  • Analyse the impact of automation on the economy and the distribution of wealth.

  Content

Automation has revolutionised industries worldwide, driving significant changes in how we live and work. It involves the use of machines, robots, and artificial intelligence (AI) to perform tasks traditionally carried out by humans. This technological advancement has led to increased efficiency and productivity across sectors, but it has also raised concerns about its broader impacts on individuals, society, and the environment. Understanding these effects is crucial to navigate the benefits and challenges posed by automation.

 

Safety of Workers

Automation has transformed industries where hazardous conditions are a daily concern. By replacing humans in dangerous tasks, automation significantly reduces the risk of injury or fatality. Robotics and AI-driven systems are used in industries such as mining, manufacturing, and construction, where high risks were once unavoidable.

  • Case Study: Mining Industry
    In the mining sector, companies like Rio Tinto have integrated autonomous haulage systems (AHS) in Australian mines. These driverless trucks reduce the risks miners face from equipment accidents, toxic environments, and cave-ins. Workers are removed from the hazardous environment and instead operate the trucks remotely. This has led to a 50% reduction in safety incidents at some sites. However, it requires workers to have new skills in technology and system management.

  • Risks of Automation: While automation improves safety, it introduces new risks related to technical malfunctions. For example, in industries using robotic arms or automated machinery, a system failure could lead to accidents if proper safety protocols aren’t in place. Furthermore, automation’s increasing complexity requires skilled human oversight to maintain and operate these systems safely.

 

Read about the Rio Tinto Autonomous Train Collision Incident here

 

 

People with Disability

Automation offers significant opportunities to improve the lives and employment prospects of people with disabilities through assistive technologies. These systems range from robotic prosthetics to AI-powered software that assists with communication, mobility, and task performance.

  • Case Study: Assistive Robotics
    Ekso Bionics, a company that develops robotic exoskeletons, enables people with mobility impairments to walk again. This innovation allows individuals who previously would have been excluded from physically demanding jobs to participate in the workforce. Voice-activated systems like Amazon's Alexa or Apple's Siri allow people with disabilities to control workspaces with minimal physical interaction, boosting independence and productivity in office settings.

  • Challenges: Despite these benefits, the rise of automation also risks excluding people with disabilities in jobs heavily reliant on routine tasks. For instance, call centres or manufacturing roles, which often employ individuals with cognitive disabilities, are increasingly automated. This raises the concern that these workers could be displaced unless retraining initiatives are prioritised to help them transition to new roles.

 

 

Skills Required for Development

Automation is reshaping the job market by displacing roles that involve repetitive or predictable tasks, while creating demand for workers skilled in new technologies such as AI, data science, and robotics. As traditional jobs disappear, workers must adapt to new roles that emphasise creative problem-solving, collaboration with machines, and technical expertise.

  • Case Study: Manufacturing Industry
    Foxconn, a leading electronics manufacturer for companies like Apple, replaced over 60,000 workers with robots at one of its plants in China in 2016. The robots performed repetitive tasks more efficiently than humans, reducing labour costs and increasing production speed. However, the company also announced that workers would be retrained for more technical jobs, such as maintaining and overseeing the robots.

  • New Skill Demands: In Australia, the agriculture industry is experiencing a similar shift. Automated harvesting machines, such as robotic fruit pickers, are being introduced to address labour shortages and improve efficiency. Farmers now need to understand how to program, operate, and repair these machines, moving away from traditional manual labour to roles requiring technical and IT skills.

  • Lifelong Learning: The shift towards automation emphasises the need for continuous reskilling and upskilling. Workers must frequently update their skill sets to stay competitive in an automated job market. This has led to an increase in training programs focused on digital literacy, robotics, and data analytics, often supported by governments or private industries.

Efficiency, Waste and Environment

Automation has brought dramatic improvements to production efficiency, leading to cost savings and higher output while reducing waste. However, it also raises environmental concerns, particularly around energy use and the ecological impact of producing automated technologies.

  • Case Study: Tesla Gigafactory
    Tesla’s Gigafactory is an excellent example of how automation can optimise production while striving for sustainability. The factory uses a combination of robotics, AI, and renewable energy to produce electric vehicle batteries at an unprecedented scale. By integrating automated systems, Tesla has drastically reduced production time and costs. The factory also aims to be powered entirely by renewable energy, minimising its environmental impact. Additionally, automation in the factory has led to significant reductions in waste, as precision manufacturing ensures minimal material loss.

  • Environmental Concerns: Despite these advances, automation can contribute to increased energy consumption, particularly when automated systems are reliant on non-renewable energy. For example, the widespread use of data centres to support automation and AI processes leads to significant energy demands. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centres consumed about 1% of the world’s electricity in 2021. Companies must invest in green technologies to ensure automation is environmentally sustainable.

  • Waste Reduction: Automation also reduces waste through precision agriculture. In Australian agriculture, automated irrigation systems and drones equipped with AI can monitor crop health and deliver water or pesticides precisely where needed, reducing water waste and the overuse of chemicals. This technology enhances both productivity and environmental sustainability.

Economy and Wealth

The economic impact of automation is profound, with both positive and negative consequences. While it drives economic growth and increases productivity, it also poses significant challenges to the fair distribution of wealth. Automation tends to disproportionately benefit capital owners and highly skilled workers, potentially widening the gap between the rich and poor.

  • Case Study: Amazon's Automated Warehouses
    Amazon uses automated systems in its warehouses to sort and ship products efficiently. Robots, such as Kiva Systems, transport goods within warehouses, reducing reliance on human labour. While this has allowed Amazon to scale rapidly, it has led to concerns over job losses and poor working conditions for the remaining human workers. Low-skilled workers are often at risk of displacement, while the wealth generated by these automated systems primarily benefits Amazon's shareholders and executives.

  • Wealth Inequality: Automation has a tendency to concentrate wealth in the hands of those who own the technology. AI and robotics companies, for example, see increased profits while workers, particularly in low-skilled jobs, are often displaced without a clear path to new employment. A 2020 study by MIT found that automation in the U.S. has contributed to wage stagnation for middle-class workers, while increasing profits for firms that deploy these technologies.

  • Policy Responses: In response, some governments are exploring policies like universal basic income (UBI) to mitigate the economic displacement caused by automation. This policy is being trialled in several countries, including Finland and Spain, as a means of providing financial security to those affected by job losses due to automation.

3.10 Human Behaviour Influences

Syllabus

Explore by implementation how patterns in human behaviour influence ML and AI software development, including:

  • psychological responses
  • patterns related to acute stress response
  • cultural protocols
  • belief systems

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Explore how patterns in human behaviour, including psychological responses, acute stress reactions, cultural protocols, and belief systems, influence the development of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) software.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Understand how psychological responses and stress-related patterns shape ML and AI system design.
  • Analyse how cultural and belief systems impact AI development.
  • Explore how these behavioural factors are incorporated into AI algorithms and systems through case studies and practical examples.

  Content

Human behaviour plays a significant role in shaping the development of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) systems. AI developers and researchers aim to create algorithms that not only analyse data but also interact effectively with users and reflect human behavioural patterns. Understanding how people respond psychologically, how stress affects decision-making, and how culture and belief systems influence behaviour is critical in designing AI systems that are ethical, user-friendly, and contextually appropriate.

 

Psychological Responses

Humans react emotionally and psychologically to technology, and these responses shape how AI systems are designed to interact with users. Factors like trust, fear, and cognitive biases are crucial considerations when building AI systems that users rely on.

Key Concepts:

  • Trust and User Adoption:

    • Users are more likely to adopt AI systems if they trust the recommendations or decisions made by the system. Trust is built through transparency (e.g., explainable AI) and reliability.

  • Fear and Resistance:

    • Psychological fear of AI, often referred to as "automation anxiety", can affect how users interact with AI systems. Developers need to create systems that feel intuitive and friendly to reduce resistance.

  • Cognitive Bias:

    • AI systems must be designed to account for human cognitive biases. For example, users may experience confirmation bias, where they favor AI outputs that confirm their pre-existing beliefs.

Example in Implementation:

In healthcare AI, systems are designed to provide transparency in their decision-making processes to build trust with medical professionals. When suggesting a diagnosis, AI systems often provide explanations for their recommendations, easing concerns that doctors may have about handing over too much control to a machine.

 

Acute Stress Response

Acute stress can significantly influence how humans interact with AI systems, especially in high-pressure environments such as emergency services or military operations. People under stress may have impaired decision-making abilities, rely more on heuristics, and exhibit fight-or-flight responses, which must be considered when designing AI that operates in these contexts.

Key Concepts:

  • Fight-or-Flight Response:
    • In stressful situations, users may need quick, simple solutions rather than complex, data-heavy recommendations. AI systems should be designed to offer straightforward, easily digestible information during critical moments.
  • Cognitive Load:
    • High-stress environments increase cognitive load—the amount of mental effort required to process information. AI systems must minimize the cognitive load on users by providing clear and concise outputs, avoiding overwhelming amounts of data.

Example in Implementation:

In AI-driven emergency response systems, like those used in disaster management, stress patterns are considered by presenting critical information in a simplified format. Visual alerts, concise instructions, and real-time updates are prioritised to help first responders make quick, informed decisions under pressure.

Cultural Protocols

Cultural diversity influences how people perceive and interact with AI systems. Developers need to consider cultural norms and practices when designing AI systems for different regions or communities to ensure the technology is respectful, acceptable, and useful across various cultural contexts.

Key Concepts:

  • Cultural Sensitivity:

    • AI systems should be tailored to align with the cultural practices and expectations of the target users. This can include language preferences, gender roles, or traditional values that differ across cultures.

  • Localisation:

    • Localisation of AI refers to adapting the system to meet the specific cultural, linguistic, and social needs of different populations. This includes language translation, cultural references, and contextually appropriate interactions.

Example in Implementation:

Voice assistants like Amazon Alexa or Google Assistant often undergo significant cultural adaptation when being deployed in different countries. For instance, these systems are programmed to recognise local dialects, respect local customs (e.g., addressing people more formally in certain cultures), and follow region-specific social norms.

 

Belief Systems

Belief systems, including religion, moral philosophies, and ethical frameworks, shape how AI systems are perceived and accepted in various societies. Developers must account for these belief systems to avoid ethical conflicts and ensure that AI systems operate within acceptable moral boundaries.

Key Concepts:

  • Ethical AI:

    • Developers must ensure that AI systems do not conflict with the ethical and moral standards of their users. For instance, certain communities may oppose AI in areas like surveillance or genetic modification based on religious beliefs.

  • Bias and Fairness:

    • AI systems must be designed to avoid bias, especially in culturally diverse societies. Developers should incorporate fairness and inclusivity into AI algorithms, ensuring that systems do not discriminate based on gender, race, religion, or other belief systems.

Example in Implementation:

In facial recognition technology, ethical AI development considers potential biases against specific racial or ethnic groups. Developers implement fairness techniques to ensure that the system works equally well across different demographics, reducing the risk of unfair treatment.

3.11 Investigating Bias

Syllabus

Investigate the effect of human and dataset source bias in the development of ML and AI solutions

  Learning Intention and Success Criteria

Learning Intention - Students will:

  • Understand how human and dataset biases can impact the development and outcomes of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) models.

Success Criteria - Students can:

  • Explain the role of human bias in AI development.
  • Describe how biases in datasets are introduced and propagated in ML models.
  • Evaluate the potential consequences of biases on AI decision-making.
  • Suggest methods to mitigate bias in AI systems.

  Content

Bias in machine learning and artificial intelligence arises when the models, data, or decisions made by developers unintentionally favour certain outcomes, groups, or perspectives over others. This can occur due to two primary factors:

  1. Human Bias – The biases held by the developers, data scientists, or organisations.
  2. Dataset Source Bias – The biases present within the data that is used to train AI models.

These biases can have profound effects on the fairness, accuracy, and inclusivity of AI systems, leading to ethical concerns and practical challenges in real-world applications.

 

Human Bias

Human bias refers to the implicit and explicit preferences, beliefs, or assumptions that developers may hold, which can influence the design and decision-making processes involved in creating AI systems. Examples include:

  • Feature Selection: The choice of variables or features for a model can reflect the developer's priorities or preconceived notions about what is important. For instance, if socio-economic status is prioritised as a feature in predictive models for employment, the model may perpetuate existing inequalities.
  • Algorithm Design: Developers might unintentionally favour certain algorithmic structures or processes that reflect their own experiences or goals, even if those structures introduce bias.
  • Labelling Bias: During the creation of datasets, humans often label data (e.g., tagging images or categorising information). Their labels may reflect personal biases, reinforcing stereotypes or errors.

 

Dataset Source Bias

 Dataset bias occurs when the data used to train machine learning models is not representative of the broader population or task. There are several ways dataset bias can be introduced:

  • Historical Bias: This occurs when the dataset reflects past inequalities or discriminations. For instance, if a hiring algorithm is trained on historical data from an industry with low gender diversity, it may learn to favour male candidates over female candidates.
  • Sampling Bias: If certain groups are overrepresented or under-represented in the dataset, the model will generalise poorly to the under-represented groups. For example, medical AI systems trained on data from one demographic may fail to accurately diagnose or recommend treatments for another.
  • Label Bias: The way data is classified or labelled can introduce biases, particularly in cases where human judgement is required, such as labelling hate speech or offensive content in social media posts. Label bias can reflect cultural or individual bias, making certain words or behaviours disproportionately flagged as problematic.

 

 

Consequences of Bias in AI Systems

The effects of human and dataset bias in AI systems can be significant, leading to:

  • Discrimination: Biased AI systems may discriminate against certain groups based on race, gender, or socio-economic status. For example, biased recruitment algorithms can perpetuate gender inequality in hiring.
  • Reduced Trust: Users and society may lose trust in AI systems if they consistently produce unfair or biased outcomes.
  • Poor Decision-Making: Bias in models can lead to inaccurate or inappropriate decisions. For example, a biased healthcare algorithm could result in misdiagnoses for under-represented populations.
  • Legal and Ethical Implications: Many countries have anti-discrimination laws, and biased AI systems could lead to legal challenges. Furthermore, there are growing concerns about the ethical responsibility of organisations deploying AI systems.

Mitigating Bias in AI Development

Several strategies can be employed to reduce bias in AI models:

  1. Diverse Teams: Building teams with diverse perspectives can help mitigate bias by ensuring that different viewpoints are considered during AI development.
  2. Bias Audits and Testing: Conducting audits and testing models for bias across different demographic groups can help identify and correct biased behaviour.
  3. Inclusive Datasets: Curating and using datasets that are representative of the entire population can help prevent dataset bias. This might include collecting additional data for under-represented groups.
  4. Algorithmic Fairness: Using fairness-aware algorithms that aim to equalise outcomes for different groups can be an effective mitigation strategy.
  5. Transparency and Accountability: Making AI models and decisions more transparent, and holding developers accountable for biased outcomes, is essential for ensuring fair AI development.

Example: Mitigating Bias in Hiring Algorithms

To reduce gender bias in hiring algorithms, companies have implemented strategies like anonymising candidate resumes (removing names and genders) and training models on more inclusive datasets that do not reflect historical gender biases.

Syllabus Spotlights

Model Answer Deconstruction

 Give a high-band sample answer.

  • Students annotate: What makes this strong? Which syllabus points are addressed?
  •  Follow-up: rewrite part of it with improvement focus (clarity, structure, evidence).

APIs

Q1. Describe the role and importance of APIs in modern software development. (3 marks)

 

High-Band Sample Answer:

An Application Programming Interface (API) acts as an intermediary layer that allows two software applications to communicate using a set of defined protocols. In modern development, APIs are essential for modularisation, enabling developers to integrate third-party services (like Stripe for payments or Google Maps for location) without writing the underlying code. This speeds up the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) and ensures consistency across different platforms.

Data Backup

Q2. Describe the process and necessity of programmed data backup. (3 marks)

 

High-Band Sample Answer:

Programmed data backup is the automated process of copying data to a secondary storage medium (e.g., off-site cloud storage or NAS) at scheduled intervals. It is a critical component of contingency planning, ensuring data integrity and availability in the event of hardware failure, cyber-attacks (like ransomware), or accidental deletion. By automating the process, developers reduce the risk of human error and ensure a reliable Recovery Point Objective (RPO).

Web Protocols

Q3. Investigate and describe the function of web protocols and their ports, including DNS and TCP/IP. (5 marks)

 

High-Band Sample Answer:

Web protocols provide the rules for data exchange across a network. TCP/IP is the fundamental suite; IP handles the addressing and routing of packets, while TCP ensures reliable delivery by establishing a connection and checking for errors. DNS (Domain Name System) functions as the "phonebook" of the internet, translating human-readable URLs (e.g., education.nsw.gov.au) into machine-readable IP addresses, typically operating on Port 53. Together, these allow data to be sent to the correct destination and reassembled accurately at the application layer.

Machine Learning

Q4. Assess the models of training Machine Learning (ML), including supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, and reinforcement learning. (8 marks)

 

High-Band Sample Answer:

The choice of training model depends heavily on the available data and the desired outcome. Supervised learning is highly effective for classification (e.g., spam filters) as it uses labelled datasets to map inputs to known outputs. In contrast, unsupervised learning is superior for pattern discovery in unlabelled data, such as market segmentation. Semi-supervised learning offers a pragmatic middle ground, using a small amount of labelled data to guide the process of a larger unlabelled set, reducing the high cost of data labelling. Finally, reinforcement learning is unique as it relies on a 'reward/penalty' system (e.g., in autonomous vehicle navigation or gaming AI). While supervised learning is more predictable, reinforcement learning is better suited for dynamic environments where the 'correct' path isn't known in advance.

 

Ethics

Q5. Investigate the effect of human and dataset source bias in the development of ML and AI solutions. (4 marks)

 

High-Band Sample Answer:

Bias in AI is often a reflection of the humans who create it or the data used to train it. Dataset source bias occurs when the training data is not representative of the real-world population (e.g., facial recognition systems trained primarily on one ethnicity). Human bias can manifest during the "feature selection" phase, where developer prejudices influence which data points the algorithm deems important. These biases lead to unfair outcomes, such as discriminatory hiring practices or biased credit scoring, highlighting the legal and ethical necessity for algorithmic transparency and diverse datasets in modern software engineering.

 

Mark the Marker

 Students are given 2 anonymised sample responses to mark against real criteria.
 Discuss where students disagree – powerful for refining exam technique.

Defensive Data Input

Question (3 marks)

Design and implement code using defensive data input handling (validation, sanitisation, error handling).

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Clearly describes all three: validation, sanitisation, and error handling with technical precision. 3
Describes two elements or provides a general overview of defensive coding. 2
Identifies one element or provides a basic definition. 1

Response A (Mid Band – likely 2–3 marks)

You should check what the user types. Use an if statement to make sure it's a number and not a word so the program doesn't crash.

Response B (Low Band – likely 1–2 marks)

Defensive coding involves validation (ensuring input meets criteria like length/type), sanitisation (stripping harmful characters like <script> tags to prevent SQL injection), and error handling (using try/except blocks) to manage unexpected inputs gracefully without crashing.

Discussion Prompts

  • What is missing from each answer in terms of software-specific consequences?

  • Which response addresses the impact on system effectiveness more clearly?

  • What would a 4-mark version of this answer look like?

Secure Code

Question (4 marks)

How would you protect user file and hardware from file attacks and side-channel attacks.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Comprehensive explanation of both file attacks and side-channel attacks with mitigation strategies. 4
Explains both types of attacks but lacks detail on hardware/file protection. 2–3
Basic identification of one attack type. 1

Response A (Mid Band)

To prevent file attacks, developers must implement strict file-type verification and 'sandboxing' to isolate uploaded content. Side-channel attacks exploit physical outputs like power consumption or electromagnetic leaks (e.g., timing attacks). Protection involves using 'constant-time' algorithms and hardware shielding to ensure the CPU doesn't leak data patterns during processing.

Response B (Low Band)

File attacks happen when a hacker uploads a virus. Side-channel attacks are when they look at how much power the computer uses or the sound the CPU makes to steal passwords. You should use encryption.

Discussion Prompts

  • What real software examples could improve these?

  • Why is Response B more informative than A?

  • What elements are missing that would push this to full marks?

Implementation Methods

Question (3 marks)

Distinguish between parallel and phased implementation methods when deploying a new software system.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Clearly distinguishes between both methods, identifying specific characteristics of each. 3
Describes both methods but lacks a clear distinction or technical detail. 2
Identifies one method or provides a general definition of implementation. 1

Response A (Mid Band)

Parallel involves running the old and new systems simultaneously, ensuring a fallback if the new system fails, though it is resource-heavy. In contrast, phased implementation introduces the new system in stages (e.g., module by module), allowing the organisation to adjust to changes gradually without the cost of running two full systems.

Response B (Low Band)

Parallel is when you run both systems at once. Phased is when you do it in stages. Direct is just turning the old one off and the new one on.

Discussion Prompts

  • What software-specific detail could improve Response A?

  • Why might Response B only get 1 mark?

  • Which words or examples would move Response A to 3 marks?

Version Control

Question (3 marks)

Explain the importance of using version control when collaborating on a software engineering project.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Provides a detailed explanation of version control benefits (e.g., branching, merging, auditing). 3
Outlines the role of version control with some technical detail. 2
Identifies a basic use of version control (e.g., "saving work"). 1

Response A (Mid Band)

Version control is vital for collaboration as it allows for branching, where developers work on features independently. It prevents code overwrites through merging and provides a 'source of truth' with an audit trail, allowing teams to revert to stable versions if bugs are introduced.

Response B (Low Band)

Version control like GitHub lets you save your code so you can go back to an old version if you break something. You use 'commit' to save.

Discussion Prompts

  • What makes Response A stronger?

  • What extra details or examples could make A a 3-mark answer?

Data Packets

Question (3 marks)

Describe the structure and role of data packets in the transmission of data over the internet.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Accurately describes the structure (header/payload) and the role of packets in transmission. 3
Provides a general description of packets without specific structural detail. 2
States that data is broken into pieces for the internet. 1

Response A (Mid Band)

Data is segmented into packets, each containing a header (source/destination IP, sequence number) and a payload (the actual data). These packets are routed independently via TCP/IP and reassembled at the destination, where the sequence numbers ensure data integrity if packets arrive out of order.

Response B (Low Band)

Data is broken into packets. They have the address on them and travel through routers until they get to the destination and join back together.

Discussion Prompts

  • Which response describes role better?

  • Which is more specific to software operations?

  • What does a high-band response look like?

Load Times

Question (4 marks)

Propose and justify two methods a developer could implement to improve the load times of a web application.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Proposes two valid methods and provides a strong justification for each (e.g., latency, file size). 4
Proposes two methods with limited justification, or one method with a strong justification. 2–3
Lists one or two general ideas for making a website faster. 1

Response A (Mid Band – likely 4 marks)

First, implement image compression and lazy loading to reduce the initial payload size and latency. Second, use a Content Delivery Network (CDN) to cache assets on servers closer to the user's geographic location. This minimises 'hops' across the network, significantly reducing the Time to First Byte (TTFB).

Response B (Low Band)

You should make the images smaller so they download faster. You could also use a faster server so the computer doesn't have to wait as long to get the files.

Discussion Prompts

  • What parts of A show justification rather than just description?

  • How could both responses add more software context?

  • What would a high-band structure for this question look like?

Webserver

Question (3 marks)

Outline the role of webserver software in managing a back-end web request.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Clearly outlines the role, including listening for requests, processing, and returning responses. 3
Describes the general function of a webserver in a client-server relationship. 2
Identifies that a webserver "hosts" a website. 1

Response A (Mid Band)

Webserver software acts as an intermediary that 'listens' for HTTP/HTTPS requests on specific ports. It handles the request-response cycle by retrieving static files or passing dynamic requests to a back-end script (like Python or PHP), then returning the appropriate status code (e.g., 200 OK) and data to the client.

Response B (Low Band)

The webserver software (like Apache) sits on the computer and waits for someone to ask for a page. When they do, it finds the file and sends it back to their browser.

Discussion Prompts

  • What kinds of technologies could be named to improve these answers?

  • Why is Response A more effective than B?

Neural Network

Question (5 marks)

Discuss the use of neural networks in designing machine learning solutions, referencing their architecture and learning process.

Marking Criteria

Criteria Marks
Comprehensive discussion covering architecture (layers/neurons) and the learning process (weights/backpropagation). 5
Describes architecture and the general idea of training with some technical detail. 3–4
Basic description of a neural network or identification of its layers. 1–2

Response A (Mid Band)

Neural networks utilise an architecture of interconnected layers (input, hidden, and output). Each connection has a weight that determines its influence. During training, the model uses backpropagation and gradient descent to adjust these weights based on the error detected in the output, allowing the system to 'learn' and improve its predictive accuracy over time.

Response B (Low Band)

Neural networks are like a brain. They have layers that process data. The more layers you have, the 'deeper' the learning is, which is why it's called deep learning.

Discussion Prompts

  • What makes A stronger than B?

  • What kind of technical information could be added to improve the answers?

  • How could A more clearly show the process of refinement?

Visual Essay Planning

 Give a complex extended response.
 In groups, sketch a mind-map or storyboard for a high-band response before writing.

Your goal: Ensure every "arm" of your mind-map connects a syllabus point to an impact (Individual, Society, or Environment).

Response 1

Stimulus and Question

Stimulus 

By 2030, it is estimated that 30% of hours worked globally could be automated. While this promises a 'Fourth Industrial Revolution' of efficiency, it also threatens to widen the gap between those who own the technology and those whose skills are displaced.

Extended Response Question (8 marks)

Assess the impact of automation on the individual, society, and the environment.

Scaffold

Range Criteria
7–8 Marks Provides a comprehensive assessment of automation's impact across all three areas (Individual, Society, Environment). Uses specific terminology and addresses all syllabus points with balanced, critical judgement.
5–6 Marks Describes several impacts of automation with some assessment. Covers most syllabus points but may lack depth in one area (e.g., environment).
3–4 Marks Outlines basic impacts of automation. Response may be more descriptive than evaluative.
1–2 Marks Identifies one or two general effects of automation (e.g., "robots take jobs").

 

Before you start writing, your group must map the following onto your poster:

  1. The Center: The core question (Impact of Automation).

  2. The Branches: The five syllabus dot points (Safety, Disability, Employment Skills, Environment/Waste, Wealth).

  3. The Links: Use different colours to show if an impact is Positive (+) or Negative (-).

  4. The "Assessment" Keywords: Words like Crucial, Detrimental, Mitigated by, or Enhanced.

 

High-Band Sample Answer (For Deconstruction)

Automation represents a paradigm shift in software engineering, moving from manual logic to autonomous systems. Its impact is multifaceted, offering significant gains in efficiency while presenting deep ethical and social challenges.

Individual Impact: Safety and Accessibility Automation significantly improves individual safety by removing humans from "Dull, Dirty, or Dangerous" tasks (e.g., robotic inspections of high-voltage power lines). Furthermore, for people with disability, automated software (like AI-driven screen readers or autonomous mobility aids) provides unprecedented independence, allowing for greater participation in the workforce and society.

Social Impact: Employment and Wealth The nature of employment is shifting; while manual roles are displaced, there is an increased demand for "high-order" skills in software maintenance, data analysis, and ethical oversight. However, without proactive policy, this risks a negative impact on the economy and distribution of wealth, as the financial gains of automation may concentrate among tech owners, potentially increasing the "digital divide" and socio-economic inequality.

Environmental Impact: Efficiency and Waste From an environmental perspective, automation enhances production efficiency, using sensors and real-time data to minimise raw material usage. However, the hardware required for these systems contributes to e-waste, and the massive energy consumption of data centres required to run complex ML models presents a new environmental challenge that engineers must address through "Green Code" practices.

Conclusion Ultimately, while automation is a tool for immense social good and environmental precision, its success depends on a transition strategy that prioritises the upskilling of workers and the equitable distribution of its economic rewards.

 Provide 5 different sample responses to the same question.
